title: [Spec Decode] Verify in head dtype and drop the FP32 chunk workaround
body:
## Purpose

Speculative decoding expands each request into multiple verification positions. Whenever
any active logits processor is present, the target rejection verifier currently
materializes an FP32 processing canvas of shape `[num_verification_tokens, vocab_size]`.
The production path bounds the transient allocation with a 1 GiB chunk, which in turn
forces a cap on the total logits adaptive verification may schedule per step.

This PR makes the target verifier explicitly opt into storing and processing logits in
the LM head dtype (BF16/FP16), and deletes the FP32 canvas, the chunk iterator, and the
adaptive cap:

- temperature is applied in FP32 when the rejection kernels, top-k/top-p, and the
  processed-logprob scorer load the logits; it is never written back to the stored
  logits;
- top-k/top-p computes its boundary in FP32 and writes back only the mask; penalties are
  computed in FP32 and written back to the head dtype with a single rounding; exact mask
  processors keep their original semantics;
- raw reporting keeps an original head-dtype snapshot only when a processor would
  overwrite the input; processed reporting reads the processed stored logits;
- the adaptive cost tables, selection formula, grammar mapping, and zero-budget contract
  are unchanged; only the hard cap that existed to serve the FP32 chunk is removed;
- the PyTorch top-p fallback's softmax and cumulative sum are pinned to FP32, since
  head-dtype target logits make the previously latent BF16 accumulation path reachable;
- speculative decoding fails closed on any nonzero `min_p`, and custom
  `logprob_token_ids` reporting is wired up.

The regular sampler, non-speculative decoding, and zero-draft steps keep the existing
FP32 processing path.

<details>
<summary>Supported sampling processors and reporting behavior</summary>

All supported processors below avoid materializing a full-vocabulary FP32 verifier canvas. This
PR does not change which processors are supported by speculative decoding.

| Sampling parameter / processor | Property | Supported in Spec Decode | Effect on stored logits | Head-dtype precision |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| temperature | Distribution scaling | Yes (unchanged) | None; consumers scale on load | Computed in FP32 |
| top_k / top_p | Selection mask | Yes (unchanged) | Preserve kept values; mask others with `-inf` | Exact |
| repetition / frequency / presence penalties | Value transformation | Yes (unchanged) | Rewrite affected values | One BF16/FP16 rounding |
| allowed_token_ids / min_tokens / bad_words | Hard token mask | Yes (unchanged) | Write `-inf` masks | Exact |
| thinking_token_budget | Forced-token override | Yes (unchanged) | Write a dtype-safe sentinel | Semantically exact |
| structured-output grammar mask | Hard token mask applied before verification | Yes (unchanged) | Write `-inf` masks | Exact |
| min_p | Probability filter | No (unchanged) | — | Any nonzero value fails validation |
| logit_bias | Additive value transformation | No (unchanged) | — | One BF16/FP16 rounding |

Raw and processed logprobs are reporting modes rather than logits processors. Raw reporting reads
a pre-processor head-dtype snapshot when stored logits may be modified. Processed reporting reads
the processed stored logits and applies temperature in FP32 on load. Adaptive-verification output
logprobs were enabled upstream by #52242 (merged 2026-08-25); this PR is rebased on top of it and
preserves its device-tensor boundary reporting through the head-dtype scorer.

</details>

Penalties are the only path that writes back to the stored logits lossily: the processor
still computes in FP32, but the result is rounded to BF16/FP16 once. Please pay
particular attention to the penalty-only, stochastic, and `top_k=1` results under
**Numerical fidelity and model quality** below. We did not find an implementation that
preserves FP32-equivalent penalty output without either reintroducing full-vocabulary
FP32 storage or adding significant extra scans/latency; this PR therefore keeps this
numerical trade-off explicit rather than claiming processed penalty logprobs are bitwise
FP32.

### Why this is not a repeat of #48641

#48641 removed the same FP32 copy and was reverted in full three days later by #49033
over a never-root-caused DP+EP+MTP hang. Beyond removing the copy, #48641 also changed
the numerics: it applied temperature by **writing the scaled values back into the
stored head-dtype logits**, for the regular sampler and the speculative verifier
alike. Every such write-back costs an extra BF16/FP16 rounding, and every downstream
consumer — rejection statistics, top-k/top-p, logprob reporting — then reads the
already-rounded, temperature-scaled values. Whether or not that contributed to the
hang, it is a real precision hazard, and this PR is built specifically to remove it:

- stored logits always keep their pre-temperature values; temperature is applied in
  FP32 registers at every load site and never touches storage;
- top-k/top-p computes its boundary in FP32 and writes back only `-inf` masks — kept
  logits are bit-identical to what the LM head produced;
- the only remaining lossy write-back is penalties, which is quantified and
  guardrailed under **Numerical fidelity and model quality** below;
- the scope is the speculative verifier only; the regular sampler keeps its FP32 path.

On the risk side, a permanent e2e test covers both #49033's pure-greedy control path
and an active path that actually enters the head-dtype verifier, in the same
distributed engine. That test guards the risk quadrant; it does not claim to reproduce
or explain the root cause of the original hang.

### Related work

- **#53090** (open) fuses only a temperature-only fast path; other processors or
  processed logprobs still fall back to the FP32 canvas, so it cannot delete the
  chunking or the adaptive cap. This PR covers every currently legal
  processor/reporting combination.
- **#50910** (merged) already adopted the "store in head dtype, upcast to FP32 and
  divide by temperature on load" contract on the draft side; this PR aligns the target
  verifier to the same contract.
- **#47808**'s `max_total_logits` cap exists only to guarantee the FP32 verifier lands
  in a single safe chunk; this PR removes that premise and does not change the adaptive
  verification algorithm.
- **#40704** is porting n-gram drafting to Model Runner V2; until it lands, n-gram
  still falls back to Model Runner V1, so the custom `logprob_token_ids` e2e request
  temporarily covers Eagle only.
- **#52242** (merged 2026-08-25, while this PR was in flight) lifted the
  adaptive-verification output-logprobs restriction. This PR is rebased on top of it:
  the device-side `cu_num_generated_tokens` boundaries it introduced are kept and flow
  through the head-dtype scorer unchanged, and removing the chunked path also removes
  the stale-layout hazard its `_verify_in_chunks` assert defended against. If
  **#52477** lands first, the grammar-mapping tests will need a rebase update.
- One acceptance criterion of **RFC #42259** is that the MRV2 path should not
  materialize avoidable full-vocabulary temporaries; the FP32 canvas this PR deletes is
  exactly such a temporary.

## Test Plan

1. Run the focused CUDA test matrix for sampling-parameter validation, sampler state,
   thinking budget, top-k/top-p, rejection sampling, adaptive verification, and the
   logprob numerical oracles and head-dtype penalty path.
2. Run the complete `test_spec_decode_logprobs` matrix across 3 speculative model setups and all
   4 `LogprobsMode` values, comparing emitted tokens and raw/processed logprob outputs with the
   non-speculative reference.
3. Run the DP2+EP+MTP regression twice. In the same distributed engine, exercise both the
   pure-greedy #49033 control signature and an active-sampling request that enters the head-dtype
   verifier; require each wave to draft and match the non-speculative output.
4. Benchmark `RejectionSampler.__call__` with BF16 logits, `K=7`, `V=129280`, and
   `R={8,256,512}` across temperature, top-p, penalties, combined processors, and logprob
   reporting. Compare p50 latency and per-call CUDA peak allocation with the FP32-canvas control.
5. Run a paired 1319-question, 5-shot GSM8K A/B evaluation covering the default path,
   penalties-only, stochastic top-p with penalties, and `top_k=1`; compare accuracy, invalid
   outputs, and acceptance length.

<details>
<summary>Repository test commands</summary>

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m pytest -q \
  tests/test_sampling_params.py \
  tests/v1/worker/test_gpu_sampler_flags.py \
  tests/v1/worker/test_gpu_thinking_budget.py \
  tests/v1/sample/test_topk_topp_sampler.py \
  tests/v1/spec_decode/test_rejection_sampler_utils.py \
  tests/v1/spec_decode/test_adaptive_verification.py \
  tests/v1/sample/test_logprobs.py::test_token_logprobs_apply_virtual_temperature
```

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m pytest -vv -s \
  tests/v1/sample/test_logprobs.py::test_spec_decode_logprobs
```

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m pytest -vv -s \
  'tests/v1/e2e/spec_decode/test_mtp_parallel_load.py::test_deepseek_mtp_load_dp[dp2]'
```

</details>

## Test Result

### Correctness and path coverage

- The targeted GPU suite passed with `231 passed, 2 skipped` (reported from the run; that console
  log was not kept). It covers every supported sampling processor, raw/processed reporting,
  adaptive verification, thinking budget and the head-dtype penalty path.
- The full public-model `test_spec_decode_logprobs` matrix passed all 3 model setups × 4
  `LogprobsMode` combinations (`12 passed`). Spec and non-spec runs returned identical emitted
  token IDs, logprob token IDs and ranks. Raw scores were bitwise equal; the largest processed-score
  difference was `0.08334`.
- The DP2+EP+MTP surrogate passed twice consecutively with a minimum spec/non-spec token match ratio
  of `1.000`. Both the pure-greedy wave matching the #49033 incident signature and the active
  sampling wave produced draft tokens, so the test covers both the control path and the new
  head-dtype verifier in the same distributed engine.
- `ruff check` and `ruff format --check` passed for all 19 changed Python files.

These results verify that the optimization is reached in production paths while preserving token
selection and logprob reporting contracts; they do not rely only on isolated kernel tests.

### Verifier memory and latency

The benchmark uses BF16 logits with `K=7`, `V=129280` and `R=512` (4096 verification rows), which
crosses the old approximately 2076-row chunk boundary. The control is the same candidate with the
head-dtype verifier disabled, so the comparison isolates this PR's verifier mode while keeping the
PyTorch top-p correctness fix on both sides.

| Processor | FP32 canvas p50 (ms) | Head dtype p50 (ms) | Per-call peak allocated |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| temperature | 5.054–5.103 | 0.979–1.093 | 1023.20 → 2.33 MiB |
| top-p | 31.178–31.219 | 25.846–26.057 | 1023.20 → 2.33 MiB |
| penalties | 11.960–12.025 | 5.316–8.148 | 1023.20 → 2.33 MiB |
| penalties + top-p | 39.058–39.361 | 30.424–34.095 | 1023.20 → 2.33 MiB |

The measured processor cases reduce the per-call allocation from 1023.20 MiB to 2.33 MiB and
improve p50 latency in every case; temperature-only is approximately five times faster. Processed
logprob reporting similarly falls from 1032.44 MiB to 20.68 MiB. This demonstrates that the FP32
canvas is removed rather than moved behind a different chunk boundary.

Raw reporting with a mutating processor is the intentional exception: preserving pre-processor
values still requires an approximately 1010 MiB BF16 snapshot, for a total around 1030.66 MiB. The
claim is therefore the removal of the verifier FP32 canvas and its local memory/latency cost, not a
general end-to-end throughput improvement.

### Numerical fidelity and model quality

Mask-only processors remain exact because kept logits are never rewritten. Temperature and top-p
processed scores have maximum finite errors of `1.91e-6` and `2.13e-4` against the FP32-input
reference, with no rank differences. Raw-reporting digests are bitwise identical between base and
head-dtype runs.

Penalties are the only lossy stored-processor path. Their FP32 calculation is rounded once on
writeback to BF16/FP16; the penalty + top-p oracle measures a maximum finite score error of
`0.0203`. We therefore evaluated all penalty-enabled combinations on the full 1319-question,
5-shot GSM8K set, in addition to the default control:

| Case | Sampling | Base | Head dtype(PR)   | Accuracy Δ | Acceptance length (base/head) |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| standard | greedy; neutral penalties(off)  | 82.942% | 82.942% | 0.000 pp | 4.2015 / 4.1509 |
| penalties-only | greedy; penalties on | 82.259% | 81.577% | −0.682 pp | 4.0394 / 4.0341 |
| stochastic | `temperature=0.7, top_p=0.9`; penalties on | 79.075% | 79.606% | +0.531 pp | 3.9586 / 3.9658 |
| `top_k=1` | `temperature=0.7, top_p=0.9`; penalties on | 82.259% | 81.653% | −0.607 pp | 3.9686 / 3.9878 |

The standard control produced identical output token sequences and correctness for all 1319
questions. Invalid counts were unchanged in every paired run. The three penalty-enabled,
fixed-seed accuracy deltas stay within ±0.682 percentage points, while their acceptance lengths
remain close to base. These are quality guardrails rather than a claim of statistical equivalence;
together with the FP32 oracle they bound the observed effect of the intentional head-dtype penalty
writeback.

## Duplicate check

Checked RFC #42259 and open PRs by issue number and relevant area keywords on 2026-08-24, and
re-checked on 2026-08-25. The only directly overlapping open PR is #53090; the scope difference is
described above.

## AI assistance

AI assistance was used for implementation, test design, GPU experiment orchestration and drafting
this description. The human submitter reviewed lines, resolved rebase conflicts and
ran the tests above, and can explain and defend the change end to end.

TORCHINDUCTOR_COMPILE_THREADS=1 TORCHINDUCTOR_CACHE_DIR=/tmp/torchinductor_root ```
### 🐛 Describe the bug With `method: ngram_gpu` + xgrammar structured outputs + `--async-scheduling`, the target model **verifies and accepts draft tokens that the grammar forbids**. The authoritative FSM then rejects them at commit time and the request is terminated: ``` ERROR [backend_xgrammar.py:162] Failed to advance FSM for request chatcmpl-... for tokens 2585. Please file an issue. ERROR [scheduler.py:1654] Unexpected: grammar rejected tokens [2585] for request chatcmpl-... Terminating request. ERROR [serving.py:173] Request chatcmpl-... failed with an internal error during generation ``` Observable behavior is strongly **concurrency-dependent** (single in-flight request is clean; the async pipeline never overlaps): | symptom | measurement | |---|---| | `/v1/chat/completions` (grammar + penalties) | **~88% HTTP 500** at concurrency 4 (bf16: 178/200; NVFP4: 87/100) | | `/v1/completions` (token-id prompts, grammar) | zero HTTP errors but **silent truncation growing with load**: mean response chars 264 → 174 → 95 → 47 → 24 → 24 at concurrency 1 → 2 → 4 → 8 → 12 → 16; server-side mean generation length collapses ~70 → ~17.5 tokens/request | | concurrency 1 | outputs intact (~264 chars, normal lengths) | | drafting itself | healthy: ~67% acceptance, ≈1.9 accepted tokens/step — the speedup potential is real, which is what makes the silent-truncation mode dangerous | ## Root-cause analysis (v0.25.1 source) Under async scheduling the engine core and the model runner end up holding **two divergent views of the draft tokens** for a structured-output request: 1. In the deferred-output path, `Scheduler.update_draft_token_ids_in_output` (`vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py`) validates drafts against the grammar (`grammar.validate_tokens`) and **patches invalid ones to `-1`** in `scheduler_output.scheduled_spec_decode_tokens`, recording the count in `num_invalid_spec_tokens`. 2. The bitmask builder (`StructuredOutputManager.grammar_bitmask`, `vllm/v1/structured_output/__init__.py`) treats a `-1` draft as "skip": it emits an **unconstrained bitmask row** for that position and sets `apply_bitmask = False` for the remainder of the window. 3. However, when ngram_gpu is used, the model runner **snapshots the *unpatched* dict** before the engine core patches it — `gpu_model_runner.py` (~line 4086): ```python # If ngram_gpu is used, we need to copy the scheduler_output to avoid # the modification has influence on the scheduler_output in engine core process. ``` so verification runs against the **original raw draft tokens**, not the grammar-filtered ones the bitmask was built for. 4. Nothing closes the gap: `num_invalid_spec_tokens` is consumed **only** by `make_spec_decoding_stats` — neither `gpu_model_runner.py` nor `rejection_sampler.py` reference it, so grammar-invalid draft positions are **never force-rejected**. Net effect: a grammar-illegal draft token is verified at an unconstrained position, accepted by the target model (it is perfectly plausible *text*), and then rejected by the authoritative FSM in `Scheduler.update_from_output` → `FINISHED_ERROR` (chat) or truncated output (token-id path). A second, compounding async-only mechanism: the 2-deep pipeline races draft validation against FSM advancement (drafts can be validated against an FSM that has not yet consumed the in-flight step's accepted tokens), which matches the observed concurrency-dependence. This half looks adjacent to PR #44993 (merged 2026-07-23, not yet in any release) — but #44993 is framed around reasoning parsers, and v0.25.1 already contains #44297 (the bonus-row fix for #44006), so what we hit appears to be an **unfixed residual specific to the ngram_gpu snapshot path**. ## Reproduction 1. Serve any model with the flags above (any nontrivial EBNF/JSON-schema grammar via xgrammar; large prompts are not required, but a grammar whose legal-token set is sparse makes it trigger faster). 2. Send ≥4 concurrent `/v1/chat/completions` requests with `structured_outputs.grammar` set and sampling enabled. 3. Watch for `Failed to advance FSM` / `grammar rejected tokens` in the engine log; HTTP 500s on chat requests; or compare output lengths at concurrency 1 vs 8 on `/v1/completions` (silent truncation). At concurrency 1 everything is clean, so smoke tests will not catch it. ## Workarounds verified - `{"method": "ngram", ...}` (CPU drafter) **with `--async-scheduling` removed** is fully correct in our testing (100/100 requests OK, no truncation, ~65% acceptance, and a −31% mean e2e latency win at our production operating point). Note plain `ngram` + `--async-scheduling` is already rejected at startup ("async scheduling is only supported with EAGLE/MTP/Draft Model/NGram GPU/DSpark"), which is what pushes users onto the broken `ngram_gpu` path in the first place. - Disabling speculative decoding obviously also avoids it. ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [Kimi K3] Add EPLB support
body:
## Summary

Add complete Kimi K3 EPLB metadata and redundant-expert support for both the main Kimi Linear model and its MTP model.

This change makes Kimi K3 expose the model-level MoE metadata expected by the v1 EPLB controller, constructs FusedMoE/MegaMoE with the physical expert layout, loads checkpoint weights into redundant physical expert slots, and keeps physical-expert metadata synchronized after a rearrangement.

The implementation is intentionally model-specific. It does not change the generic EPLB policy, communication implementation, or scheduling algorithm.

## Why this change is needed

Before this PR, Kimi K3 instantiated its MoE layers without exposing the complete `MixtureOfExperts` contract used by EPLB:

- the model did not report its MoE layer list to `EplbState`;
- logical, physical, redundant, and rank-local expert counts were not tracked consistently;
- FusedMoE was not constructed with Kimi's EPLB/redundant-expert configuration;
- MegaMoE only allocated the original logical experts;
- checkpoint expert mappings did not populate redundant physical slots;
- the MTP MoE container did not register its expert layers with EPLB.

As a result, the generic EPLB controller could not safely build and update Kimi K3 expert maps.

## Implementation

### Main Kimi K3 model

`vllm/models/kimi_k3/nvidia/model.py` now:

1. Derives the expert layout from the runtime parallel configuration:

   - `n_logical_experts` remains the checkpoint/model expert count;
   - `n_redundant_experts` comes from `EPLBConfig` when EPLB is enabled;
   - `n_physical_experts = n_logical_experts + n_redundant_experts`;
   - `n_local_physical_experts = n_physical_experts / ep_size`.

2. Validates physical-expert divisibility only for paths that require it: MegaMoE or EPLB. This avoids changing ordinary non-EPLB FusedMoE behavior.

3. Constructs MegaMoE with the physical expert count and correct rank-local physical range.

4. Constructs FusedMoE with:

   ```python
   enable_eplb=self.enable_eplb
   num_redundant_experts=self.n_redundant_experts
   ```

5. Includes redundant physical slots in `fused_moe_make_expert_params_mapping`, so every redundant replica receives its initial logical-expert checkpoint weights.

6. Adds `KimiK3MixtureOfExperts`, which exposes the model-level metadata required by EPLB:

   - `moe_mlp_layers`;
   - `moe_layers`;
   - `num_moe_layers`;
   - logical/physical/local/redundant expert counts;
   - routed/shared expert counts;
   - expert-group count.

7. Implements `update_physical_experts_metadata()` so the model and individual Kimi MoE layers remain synchronized when the physical layout changes.

8. Makes `KimiLinearForCausalLM` implement this shared Kimi K3 MoE interface and registers every real, non-PP-placeholder Kimi MoE layer.

### MTP model

`vllm/models/kimi_k3/nvidia/mtp.py` now:

- makes `KimiK3MTP` implement `KimiK3MixtureOfExperts`;
- registers all MTP MoE layers with the same metadata path as the main model;
- includes redundant expert slots when constructing the MTP checkpoint expert mapping.

This keeps main-model and MTP expert registration consistent without duplicating EPLB bookkeeping logic.

## Expert layout example used in validation

The full Kimi K3 checkpoint contains 896 logical routed experts.

With EPLB enabled in the validation run:

```text
logical experts:    896
redundant experts:   16
physical experts:   912
EP size:              16
physical slots/rank:  57
```

The control run retained the original identity layout:

```text
logical experts:    896
redundant experts:    0
physical experts:   896
EP size:              16
physical slots/rank:  56
```

## End-to-end validation configuration

Two full GSM8K runs were executed. They used the same model, image, hardware topology, parallelism, model limits, weight-loading configuration, and request workload. The functional difference was whether EPLB rearrangement was enabled.

| Setting | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Model | `moonshotai/Kimi-K3` |
| Model revision | `79a424f302e6ed63cd82211b0e99918cdb6de8df` |
| Runtime image | `kimi-k3-oss-0723-arm64-cu130-ubuntu2404-commit-e3e837.sqsh` |
| Service nodes | 4 × GB200 nodes, 4 GPUs/node |
| Client node | 1 additional node |
| Tensor parallelism | TP4 |
| Data parallelism | DP4 |
| Expert parallelism | EP16 |
| GPU memory utilization | 0.85 |
| MTP | disabled for this main-model comparison |
| GSM8K test questions | 1319 |
| Few-shot examples | 5 |
| Client concurrency | 128 |
| Maximum output tokens | 1024 |
| Maximum model length | 2944 |
| Maximum sequences | 256 |
| Weight loader | `fastsafetensors` |
| Safetensors strategy | `lazy` |
| `VLLM_FASTSAFETENSORS_QUEUE_SIZE` | 1 |
| EPLB load window | 32 steps |
| EPLB rearrangement interval | 64 steps |
| EPLB policy | `default` |
| EPLB communicator | `torch_gloo` |
| EPLB mode | synchronous (`use_async=false`) |

Exact EPLB-enabled configuration:

```json
{
  "window_size": 32,
  "step_interval": 64,
  "num_redundant_experts": 16,
  "log_balancedness": true,
  "log_balancedness_interval": 16,
  "use_async": false,
  "policy": "default",
  "communicator": "torch_gloo"
}
```

Exact observation-only control configuration:

```json
{
  "window_size": 32,
  "step_interval": 64,
  "num_redundant_experts": 0,
  "log_balancedness": true,
  "log_balancedness_interval": 16,
  "use_async": false,
  "policy": "default",
  "communicator": "torch_gloo"
}
```

The control retained the load-accounting instrumentation and identity expert map but performed no expert rearrangement, weight movement, or map commit.

## Full GSM8K results

| Metric | EPLB enabled (job 10272) | Observation-only control (job 10300) | Interpretation |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Correct answers | 1260 / 1319 | 1256 / 1319 | Four-answer difference |
| Accuracy | 95.5269% | 95.2237% | 0.3032 percentage-point difference |
| Request errors | 0 | 0 | Both runs completed cleanly |
| Evaluation latency | 1466.50 s | 463.11 s | Synchronous rearrangement dominates EPLB wall time |
| Questions/s | 0.8994 | 2.8481 | Control is 3.17× faster |
| Output tokens/s | 91.37 | 291.66 | Control is 3.19× faster |
| Rank-load samples | 97 | 97 | Same observation cadence |
| Median rank balancedness | 0.9919 | 0.9356 | EPLB substantially improves rank balance |
| High-load median balancedness | 0.9947 | 0.9374 | Same conclusion under sustained load |
| Median max/mean rank load | 1.008× | 1.069× | EPLB reduces the hottest-rank excess |
| Completed formal rearrangements | 24 | 0 | Profile rearrangement excluded |
| Rank-level map commits | 384 | 0 | 24 rearrangements × 16 EP ranks |

### Rank-load metric

The figure and reported balancedness use the raw 16-rank arrays emitted by the experiment:

```text
[EPLB_TRACE] rank_load ... rank_tokens=[rank0, ..., rank15]
```

Rank balancedness is calculated as:

```text
mean(rank_tokens) / max(rank_tokens)
```

This is deliberately calculated from `rank_tokens` rather than reusing the generic `EPLB step: balancedness=...` log field, because this experiment specifically measures aggregate EP-rank imbalance.

### Rearrangement cost

The EPLB run produced 24 formal `committed=True` rearrangements during the evaluation:

- cumulative CUDA-event-measured rearrangement time: **933.8124 seconds**;
- median rearrangement duration: **38.88 seconds**;
- maximum rearrangement duration: **39.87 seconds**;
- total EPLB evaluation wall time: **1466.50 seconds**;
- control evaluation wall time: **463.11 seconds**;
- wall-time difference: **1003.39 seconds**.

The measured rearrangement GPU time is 63.7% of the EPLB run's complete wall time and is close to the observed wall-time difference. The CUDA-event value is not claimed to be a complete wall-clock measurement: CPU coordination, collectives, and scheduling can add additional time.

Because this run used `use_async=false`, every rearrangement was on the synchronous inference path:

```text
EplbState.step()
  -> EplbState.rearrange()
  -> rearrange_expert_weights_inplace()
  -> commit expert maps
  -> resume forward execution
```

The generic EPLB implementation also has an asynchronous worker mode, but async EPLB was not evaluated in these two runs and no async performance claim is made here.

## Timeline and comparison image

![Kimi K3 EPLB GSM8K comparison](https://github.com/aoshen02/vllm/blob/806149b88868cda5afac8405437f1124caa3d1a2/docs/eplb/kimi-k3-eplb-gsm8k-comparison.png?raw=true)

The red bands are the 24 formal synchronous rearrangement periods. Each band is labelled with the CUDA-event duration from its corresponding `committed=True` log entry. The lower panel shows the cumulative measured GPU rearrangement time.

The figure intentionally omits separate throughput and latency bar charts; all exact end-to-end values are listed in the results table above.

## Uploaded experiment record

A detailed, repository-backed experiment record is included here:

- [`docs/eplb/kimi-k3-eplb-gsm8k-experiment.md`](https://github.com/aoshen02/vllm/blob/806149b88868cda5afac8405437f1124caa3d1a2/docs/eplb/kimi-k3-eplb-gsm8k-experiment.md)
- [`docs/eplb/kimi-k3-eplb-gsm8k-comparison.png`](https://github.com/aoshen02/vllm/blob/806149b88868cda5afac8405437f1124caa3d1a2/docs/eplb/kimi-k3-eplb-gsm8k-comparison.png)

Local raw artifacts retained for reproducibility:

- EPLB server log: `/home/inf-aoshen/vllm/projects/vllm-rl-day0-support/k3/agent_run/results/k3-full-gsm8k-eplb-load-10272/serve-srun.log`
- Control server log: `/home/inf-aoshen/vllm/projects/vllm-rl-day0-support/k3/agent_run/results/k3-full-gsm8k-eplb-load-10300/serve-srun.log`
- EPLB GSM8K summary: `/home/inf-aoshen/vllm/projects/vllm-rl-day0-support/k3/agent_run/results/k3-full-gsm8k-eplb-load-10272/gsm8k-full.json`
- Control GSM8K summary: `/home/inf-aoshen/vllm/projects/vllm-rl-day0-support/k3/agent_run/results/k3-full-gsm8k-eplb-load-10300/gsm8k-full.json`
- EPLB load analysis: `/home/inf-aoshen/vllm/projects/vllm-rl-day0-support/k3/agent_run/results/k3-full-gsm8k-eplb-load-10272/load-imbalance.json`
- Control load analysis: `/home/inf-aoshen/vllm/projects/vllm-rl-day0-support/k3/agent_run/results/k3-full-gsm8k-eplb-load-10300/load-imbalance.json`
- Plot generator: `/home/inf-aoshen/vllm/projects/vllm-rl-day0-support/k3/agent_run/scripts/plot_eplb_comparison.py`
- Experiment launcher: `/home/inf-aoshen/vllm/projects/vllm-rl-day0-support/k3/agent_run/scripts/run_k3_full_gsm8k_eplb_load_imbalance.sbatch`

## Limitations and follow-up work

- The current `rank_load` window aggregates prefill and decode tokens. It does not yet produce separate prefill-only and decode-only imbalance statistics.
- This comparison validates synchronous EPLB only. Async EPLB requires a separate experiment.
- The observation-only load accounting used for the control run was an experiment overlay and is not part of this model-support PR.
- The runtime experiments used the PR commit as their model-support baseline plus temporary observability instrumentation. The PR itself remains limited to the Kimi K3 model/MTP support and the uploaded experiment documentation.
- The comparison demonstrates that the rearrangement algorithm improves rank balance, but the tested `step_interval=64` synchronous configuration is too expensive for this workload. This is a configuration/runtime-policy result, not a correctness failure in the Kimi K3 registration patch.

## Validation

Implementation checks completed before the original PR commit:

```bash
python -m py_compile vllm/models/kimi_k3/nvidia/model.py
python -m py_compile vllm/models/kimi_k3/nvidia/mtp.py
pre-commit run
```

Documentation/image commit checks:

```bash
git diff --check
pre-commit run --files \
```
