The user explicitly authorized this draft for review and assessment by vLLM collaborators. Human line-by-line review and independent validation are still pending; this draft is not presented as merge-ready.

title: [Core] Add cache-aware admission ordering
body:
## Purpose

Within a bounded look-ahead window over the waiting queue, admit requests whose prefix is
already resident in the KV cache ahead of requests that would have to compute theirs.

The problem is an interaction between strict FCFS admission and prefix caching: a cold
request admitted first allocates blocks, and under pressure that allocation evicts blocks
which a request further back in the queue still needs. The eviction turns a would-be cache
hit into recomputation, and the deeper the shared prefix, the more expensive the loss.
Looking a bounded distance ahead lets the scheduler admit the resident request first, so
the cold request's allocation no longer destroys reuse that was about to be collected.

Two new scheduler options, both off by default:

| Flag | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--cache-aware-admission-window N` | 0 | Look-ahead depth over the waiting queue; 0 admits strictly in arrival order |
| `--cache-aware-admission-threshold F` | 0.0 | KV cache usage below which the window is not applied |

Deliberate limits on scope:

- Reordering is confined to the window, and within it to the slots held by plain
  `WAITING` requests with nothing computed. A request in a blocked status
  (`WAITING_FOR_REMOTE_KVS` and friends) or one already partially computed keeps its exact
  position, and nothing is moved past it. This is a reordering among peers, not a change
  in priority.
- It requires the `fcfs` policy. Positional reordering is meaningless in a priority heap —
  `PriorityRequestQueue.prepend_request` re-inserts by priority and ignores position — and
  it would also fight the user's explicit priorities. Under `priority` the feature is
  disabled at construction.
- It requires prefix caching, and is skipped on steps that defer prefill anyway.
- The threshold exists so operators can confine reordering to periods where there are
  evictions worth avoiding. It defaults to 0.0 (always apply) so that setting only the
  window has a visible effect rather than silently doing nothing on a roomy cache.

Scoring uses a new `KVCacheManager.get_num_cached_tokens`, which probes the cache without
taking references, allocating blocks, or emitting events, so it is safe to call for a
request that may not be scheduled. `get_computed_blocks` is unsuitable for this: it emits
`BlockStored` events under `kv_cache_report_mode="full"`, which would publish phantom
events for requests that were only scored.

Cost is one prefix-cache lookup per request in the window per step, plus one linear pass
over the waiting queue when the order actually changes.

## Why this is not duplicating an existing PR

**#53571** (SLO-aware scheduling policy) is the closest existing work and deserves an
explicit comparison, since it also reorders waiting requests. It is keyed on TTFT targets
and prompt length, to stop short prompts queueing behind long prefills; this is keyed on
resident prefix length, to stop cold admissions evicting reusable blocks. Different
signal, different objective, and they could coexist.

The implementations diverge deliberately. #53571 adds a new `SchedulingPolicy` value,
which makes it mutually exclusive with `priority`. This is a bounded per-step re-sort
behind its own flag, so it composes with whatever policy is in force rather than replacing
it. If maintainers would prefer these unified under one policy mechanism, I am glad to
adapt.

Other adjacent open PRs, none overlapping:

- **#54327** (bounded prefix-aware filesystem cache eviction) concerns the KV-offload
  filesystem tier, not admission order.
- **#53772** and **#54348** rework promotion of blocked `skipped_waiting` requests. This
  PR pins non-`WAITING` requests in place, so it composes; the status filter is covered by
  the tests.
- **#45558** (priority-based preemption at `max_num_seqs`) preempts running requests; this
  never preempts.

Checks run (`gh` was not authenticated in my environment, so these were run against the
public search API; the equivalent `gh` invocations are):

```bash
gh pr list --repo vllm-project/vllm --state open --search "cache-aware admission"
gh pr list --repo vllm-project/vllm --state open --search "prefix cache admission order"
gh pr list --repo vllm-project/vllm --state open --search "waiting queue reorder"
```

## Test Plan

Five new tests in `tests/v1/core/test_scheduler.py`, built on a helper that seeds the
prefix cache with one request's prompt so a later request is genuinely warm:

- `test_cache_aware_admission_prefers_cached_prefix` — the warm request is admitted ahead
  of the cold one that arrived first.
- `test_cache_aware_admission_does_not_look_past_the_window` — a warm request outside the
  window keeps its place in arrival order.
- `test_cache_aware_admission_skipped_below_threshold` — below the usage threshold,
  admission stays in arrival order.
- `test_cache_aware_admission_requires_fcfs_and_prefix_caching[priority, no-caching]` —
  the feature is off under the `priority` policy and with prefix caching disabled.

`create_scheduler` gains `cache_aware_admission_window`, `cache_aware_admission_threshold`
and `policy` parameters.

## Test Result

All green. Commands and results:

```
pytest tests/v1/core/test_scheduler.py \
       tests/v1/core/test_prefix_caching.py               253 passed  (5 new)
pytest tests/v1/core/test_scheduler.py \
       tests/v1/core/test_async_scheduler.py \
       tests/v1/core/test_priority_preemption_bug.py      180 passed
```

Environment note: the host for these runs has no `torch`, so tests ran inside the
`vllm/vllm-openai-rocm:nightly` image (vllm `0.28.1rc1.dev108+g1dc464d42`, torch 2.12.0,
Python 3.12) with this checkout's sources overlaid on the installed package, whose build
is a direct ancestor of this branch. This deviates from the `uv`/`.venv` workflow in
`AGENTS.md`; I intend to re-run under the standard workflow before merge.

A single pytest process over all of `tests/v1/core` is SIGKILLed partway through on this
machine, on `main` as well as on this branch, so the suite was run per-file. Each file
passes on its own.

## Serving results

Kimi-K3 FP4, 8x MI355X, a single engine with DCP=8, replaying an agentic-coding trace.
Interactivity is per-user output speed at the 90th percentile; higher is better.

### 1. Window in isolation (cadence held constant)

The claim attributable to *this* PR. Both arms pin `prefill_schedule_interval=29` and
`sched_stats=1`; the only difference is the admission window. Concurrency 52, 3628s and
3625s, same day a few hours apart.

| `cache_aware_admission_window` | p90 interactivity | tok/s/GPU | server prefix-cache hit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 12.56 | 7,983 | 90.7% |
| 16 | 12.80 (+1.96%) | 8,339 (+4.47%) | 91.5% (+0.8pp) |

A repeat at `window=16` under the identical configuration gives 12.77 and 8,459 tok/s/GPU,
so the direction reproduces. The gain is small and the arms are not repeated enough to put
a tight interval on it; I would describe it as a low-single-digit improvement in both
metrics, with the prefix-cache hit rate moving the way the mechanism predicts — that last
point is what makes the other two deltas credible rather than coincidental.

### 2. Across concurrency, deployed configuration

The configuration actually deployed enables this PR's window together with
`prefill_schedule_interval` from #54627, against a baseline with both absent. These
figures are for the two options together, not for this change in isolation. LMCache KV
offload, 3600s measured window.

| concurrency | window / interval | baseline p90 interactivity | with both options |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 44 | 64 / 33 | 11.94 | 17.28 (+44.7%) |
| 48 | 64 / 33 | 11.32 | 16.33 (+44.3%) |
| 52 | 64 / 33 | 10.98 | 13.27 (+20.8%) |

Throughput over the same runs is close to unchanged, as expected for a change that
reorders admission rather than removing work: 9,617 to 9,390 tok/s/GPU at concurrency 44
(−2.4%), 10,537 to 10,103 at 48 (−4.1%), and 8,001 to 8,409 at 52 (+5.1%).

### 2b. How the benefit tracks with concurrency

Same two options, measured across the concurrency range rather than at one point.
Each concurrency runs in its own published configuration -- concurrency 44 and 48 use
DCP8 with KV offload and no speculative decoding, 14 and 1 use DCP1 with MTP -- so this
is the benefit in each deployment as it is actually run, not one configuration swept
across load.

| concurrency | baseline | with both options |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 48 | 11.32 | 16.33 (+44.3%) |
| 44 | 11.94 | 17.28 (+44.7%) |
| 14 | 46.65 | 46.79 (+0.3%) |
| 1 | 121.47 | 121.95 (+0.4%) |

The benefit is concentrated at high concurrency and disappears at low concurrency, which
is what both mechanisms predict. Admission ordering only matters when there is a waiting
queue to reorder, and a prefill cadence only matters when prefill and decode are
contending for the same steps. At concurrency 1 and 14 the queue is shallow or empty and
there is little for either option to act on, so the deltas sit at a few tenths of a
percent -- within run-to-run noise, and reported here to show the absence of an effect
rather than to claim one.

### 3. Window sizing

A same-day sweep varying **only** the window, with the prefill cadence and threshold
pinned across all three arms. Concurrency 52, ~3600s per arm.

| `cache_aware_admission_window` | p90 interactivity | tok/s/GPU | prefix-cache hit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 16 | 13.08 | 8,298 | 96.93% |
| 64 | 13.01 | 8,349 | 96.92% |
| 128 | 13.13 | 8,317 | 97.02% |

**The size is immaterial over an 8x range.** p90 spans 13.01-13.13 and throughput
8,298-8,349 — about 1%, inside run-to-run noise on this workload, with no monotonic
trend.

The mechanism explains why. Admission reorders scale 1,220 to 1,581 going from window 16
to 64 and then saturate: 128 gives 1,584, i.e. 0.2% more. This trace's waiting queue
averages about 20 deep and peaks near 70, so a window of 64 already spans it and widening
further has nothing left to reorder.

That also answers the cost question directly: since a larger window buys nothing
measurable, there is no reason to run one. Prefer the smallest window that spans the usual
queue depth. Combined with the threshold defaulting to 0.5, the per-step probe is bounded
both by width and by only running under pressure.

### Input-length coverage

ISL is a property of the agentic workload, not a knob. The trace is replayed
request-for-request, so ISL arrives as a heavy-tailed distribution and every run sweeps
that distribution rather than sitting at one length. Reporting a single "ISL"
number for an agentic trace would be misleading: the mean is roughly 120k tokens, but it
is pulled there by the tail, and the median request is only about 84k.

Per-run distributions, showing what each measurement actually covers:

| run | n | ISL mean | p50 | p75 | p90 | p95 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| conc 44 baseline | 2,462 | 117,173 | 84,644 | 135,675 | 241,476 | 340,419 |
| conc 44 both options | 2,377 | 118,084 | 84,302 | 136,698 | 245,376 | 343,461 |
| conc 48 baseline | 2,567 | 122,854 | 83,905 | 140,551 | 253,786 | 374,550 |
| conc 48 both options | 2,400 | 125,888 | 84,096 | 142,877 | 259,991 | 469,672 |

Three things follow from this that matter for reading the results above:

1. **Coverage.** Each arm spans roughly 84k at the median to 250k at p90, with the top 5%
   reaching 340k-470k. So the reported deltas are already integrated over a 3-5x span of
   input length, not measured at one point on it.
2. **Fairness.** The distributions are closely matched between the arms being compared —
   medians agree within 0.9% and p90s within 2.5% — so the A/B is not confounded by one
   arm drawing easier requests.
3. **Where the options should act.** Admission ordering and prefill cadence matter most
   where prefill work is large relative to a decode step, which is the upper half of this
   distribution. A fixed-ISL sweep at, say, 8k would sit far below the median and would
   not exercise the mechanism this PR targets.

Output lengths are short and similarly matched (median 278-301 tokens, p90 1,738-1,845),
which is what makes interactivity the metric of interest here rather than throughput.

If a fixed-ISL sweep would still be useful, that is a different experiment — synthetic
fixed-length requests rather than trace replay — and I am happy to run it; ISL is simply
not an independent variable in the measurement above.

An earlier revision of this section reported results against the `vllm-simple` KV offload
backend. That backend is no longer what we run.

No accuracy eval was run. Neither the model computation nor sampling is touched; the
change affects only the order in which waiting requests are admitted. Batch composition
does change, as with any scheduling change, so outputs are not bit-identical. I am happy
to run `tests/evals` or a gsm8k pass if reviewers would like that confirmed.

## AI assistance

AI assistance (Cursor) was used to write this change, its tests and this description. I
have reviewed every changed line and can defend the design.

title: [Spec Decode] Fix Hybrid Mamba KV-cache admission for dynamic K
body:
## Summary

Fix a correctness issue in Hybrid Mamba KV-cache admission when the existing scheduler selects a dynamic speculative-token count (`K`) based on the current batch size.

The scheduler already supports dynamic `K`, but Mamba state admission was still accounted using the maximum `K`. This over-reserved KV-cache capacity and caused avoidable request queuing under concurrent workloads.

This PR makes admission, allocation, lookahead allocation, and `SchedulerOutput` use the same step-level `K` selected by the scheduler. It does not introduce a new dynamic-`K` policy.

## Motivation

Before this fix, the scheduler could select a smaller `K` for larger batches, while Mamba admission continued to reserve state for the maximum `K`. The resulting accounting mismatch reduced the number of requests admitted per iteration and created unnecessary waiting, especially at concurrency 16 and 32.

## Changes

- Use the scheduler's current step-level `K` for Mamba KV-cache admission.
- Propagate the same `K` through allocation and lookahead allocation.
- Keep `SchedulerOutput` consistent with the admission decision.
- Preserve the existing dynamic-`K` selection policy.
- Add focused unit tests for Mamba admission accounting and scheduler dynamic-`K` consistency.

## Validation

### Unit tests

`8 passed`

The tests cover:

- Mamba admission block accounting.
- Consistency of dynamic `K` across the scheduler, allocation, lookahead allocation, and `SchedulerOutput`.

These tests validate correctness invariants. The end-to-end benchmark below measures the resulting scheduler behavior and throughput.

### End-to-End Throughput

Both runs used the same protocol:

- Qwen3.5-4B with DFlash
- Input/output length: 1024/256
- Closed-loop streaming workload
- `settle=first C completions`
- `N=max(256, 8C)`
- `max_num_batched_tokens=16384`
- `max_num_seqs=128`
- Prefix caching disabled
- Eager execution enabled
- Seed 42

| Concurrency | Before (tokens/s) | After (tokens/s) | Improvement |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 16 | 414.76 | 752.60 | +81.5% |
| 32 | 392.23 | 950.20 | +142.3% |

Request throughput improved from 1.6202 to 2.9399 req/s at concurrency 16, and from 1.5321 to 3.7117 req/s at concurrency 32.

### Steady-State Scheduler Capacity

The following values are summarized from 10-second server-metric samples after each concurrency point completed its settling phase. Startup ramp-up samples and final drain samples are excluded. Values are reported as observed steady-state ranges, rather than maximum values over the entire run.

| Concurrency | Before: running / waiting | After: running / waiting | Before: KV usage | After: KV usage |
| ---: | :--- | :--- | ---: | ---: |
| 16 | 7-8 / 7-8 (typically 8 / 8) | 14-16 / 0 (typically 16 / 0) | 80-91% | 45-53% |
| 32 | 7-8 / 24 (typically 8 / 24) | 27-31 / 0-3 | 79-91% | 87-100% |

At concurrency 16, the fix allows the scheduler to sustain approximately twice as many running requests without a waiting queue. At concurrency 32, the scheduler reaches the available KV-cache limit while keeping the waiting queue small and transient.

## Scope

This PR fixes the accounting mismatch between the existing dynamic-`K` policy and Hybrid Mamba admission. It does not add a new capacity-adaptation algorithm or change the scheduler's dynamic-`K` policy.

title: [Test][Core] Cover Mamba-deferred prefix-cache metrics
body:
## Purpose

Add scheduler regression coverage for the Mamba same-step cache deferral path
after #48860 moved prefix-cache statistics recording from lookup time to request
admission.

Hybrid attention/Mamba requests can be looked up more than once when a Mamba
state block cached by a sibling request in the same scheduler step temporarily
prevents admission. These retries are not preemptions. The new test verifies
that each request and its prompt tokens are counted exactly once despite those
repeated lookups.

The existing hybrid scheduler helper is generalized so the test can select
`mamba_cache_mode="align"` without attaching a KV connector.

## Why this is not a duplicate

No open PR references #48860 or covers Mamba same-step deferral for
prefix-cache metrics. #48970 tests hybrid-Mamba output correctness for #43559
with GPU end-to-end workloads; it does not test scheduler metric accounting.
#48668 fixed statistics dropped by zero-output offline-engine steps, whereas
this test guards against repeated lookup accounting before admission.

## Test plan and results

On a Linux CPU pod at `d8f840071`:

```bash
PYTHONPATH=/local-ssd/vllm .venv/bin/python -m pytest \
  tests/v1/core/test_scheduler.py -v \
  -k "prefix_cache_query_not_inflated or preemption_re_records_prefix_cache_query or prefix_cache_stats_not_recorded_when_caching_disabled or external_prefix_cache_metrics or hybrid_per_group_hit_divergence or hybrid_fa_deeper_hit"
```

Result: `13 passed, 135 deselected`.

The new test also passed after restoring the current implementation. For a
negative control, moving statistics recording back to lookup time as before
#48860 made it fail with `(requests, queries) == (5, 256)` instead of the
expected `(3, 144)`.

```bash
uvx ruff check tests/v1/core/test_scheduler.py
uvx ruff format --check tests/v1/core/test_scheduler.py
git diff --check
```

All checks passed. Model evaluation does not apply because this change only
adds unit-test coverage and does not modify runtime code or model output.

title: [Core] Add per-request prefix-cache write policy
body:
## Purpose

Fixes #51234.

Add a per-request `skip_writing_prefix_cache` policy. A request can still reuse existing prefix-cache entries, but newly computed blocks from that request are not admitted to either the local GPU prefix cache or the native CPU KV offload cache.

This is useful for mixed workloads such as:

```text
[reusable system/tool prefix] + [one-off RAG document or tool output]
```

The shared prefix remains reusable, while low-reuse suffixes do not accumulate and evict hotter prefixes.

## Method

The policy is carried through OpenAI Chat/Completions/Responses, Anthropic Messages, batch chat, streaming updates, and online/offline beam search.

The implementation covers:

- synchronous local prefix-cache insertion;
- async delayed local cache commits;
- native `OffloadingConnector` normal chunk stores;
- aligned-boundary and partial-tail native offload stores.

Cache reads remain enabled. Required KV transport such as prefill/decode handoff is unchanged because the new offload guard is scoped to optional native cache-persistence paths.

## Benchmark

```bash
.venv/bin/python benchmarks/benchmark_prefix_cache_admission.py
```

The deterministic CPU benchmark seeds eight reusable hot prompts, then mixes in 64 one-off RAG-style requests. Each cold request reuses a 4-block common prefix and has a unique 24-block suffix. The cache has 159 usable blocks; an active cold request fits beside the complete hot cache, so this measures admission pollution rather than unavoidable active-request pressure.

| Policy | Hot hit rate | Hot tokens recomputed | Cold hit rate | Cached hashes |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Admit all | 27.3% | 11,904 | 14.3% | 158 |
| Cold requests no-store | **100.0%** | **0** | 14.3% | 100 |

No-store saves 11,904 hot-prefix prefill tokens while preserving cold requests' shared-prefix hits. With a large 512-block cache both policies reach 100% hot hits, confirming the benefit appears specifically under cache-capacity contention.

## Tests

Automated verification after rebasing onto the latest `main`:

- `tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/offloading_connector/test_scheduler.py`: **314 passed**
- `tests/v1/core/test_prefix_caching.py` plus the OpenAI request-policy suite: **165 passed**
- Anthropic pass-through focused test: passed
- `ruff check`, `ruff format --check`, and `git diff --check`: passed
- Prefix-cache admission benchmark reproduced the table above

## Accountability

Duplicate checks found no other open PR for #51234 or `skip_writing_prefix_cache`.

AI assistance was used. The human submitter will review every changed line and rerun the relevant tests before merge.

title: [Bugfix][Core] Count the external claim's state block in MambaManager admission
body:
## Purpose

Fix the wrong `num_new_blocks` calculation in `MambaManager.get_num_blocks_to_allocate` (align mode) when a KV connector cache hit is loaded synchronously on a hybrid model with Mamba/GDN layers (`--mamba-cache-mode align`). The estimate is one block short per Mamba group, so the request is admitted with `free == estimate` and the pool raises inside the allocation, killing the EngineCore:

```
File "vllm/v1/core/kv_cache_coordinator.py", line 299, in allocate_new_blocks
File "vllm/v1/core/single_type_kv_cache_manager.py", line 1882, in allocate_new_blocks
    new_blocks = self.block_pool.get_new_blocks(num_new_blocks)
File "vllm/v1/core/block_pool.py", line 681, in get_new_blocks
ValueError: Cannot get 1 free blocks from the pool
```

Cause: the align-mode estimate caps `num_new_blocks` at what `allocate_new_blocks` pulls, but when external computed tokens and new tokens are allocated in the same `allocate_slots` call, the inherited `allocate_external_computed_blocks` pulls the boundary state block first, and that block is not counted. Async loads are unaffected (the external span is allocated with no new tokens) and #57050 only fixed the over-estimate in the same function, so this is still present on `main`.

Fix: count the blocks `allocate_external_computed_blocks` will pull (`cdiv(total_computed, block_size) - max(skipped, held)`) and size the `allocate_new_blocks` share from the blocks held after it. The estimate then equals the allocation for sync loads and stays exact for async loads and cold prefills.

### Supersedes #46892

#46892 (thanks @zqs164) found the same bug and was approved by @MengqingCao and @ivanium in June, but pre-commit failed, it has needed a rebase since #57050 rewrote the cap in July, and there has been no activity on it since — the bug is still live on `main` three months later and kills the engine whenever a KV connector loads a cache hit synchronously on a Mamba/GDN hybrid in align mode, which is why we are opening a new PR rather than waiting on it. It also takes a different approach rather than rebasing #46892:

- #46892 adds a constant `+1` inside the cap. That is exact only when the claim ends on a block boundary; for a mid-block claim (e.g. 133 external + 11 new tokens with block size 16) it reserves a block that is never pulled, one per Mamba group, which can refuse a request that fits near the pool ceiling. This change counts the actual pull, so admission equals allocation in both cases (the invariant `test_mamba_checkpoint_admission_matches_allocation` asserts).
- The external block is counted outside `physical_block_cap`, which only describes `allocate_new_blocks`, so the fix does not depend on the cap's formula (the coupling that made #46892 conflict with #57050).
- "External tokens present" is tested with `total_computed_tokens > num_local_computed_tokens` instead of `len(new_computed_blocks) * block_size`, which also holds under partial local hits.

The `request_id not in self.num_cached_block` gate suggested in #46892's review is kept.

## Test Plan

```
pytest tests/v1/core/test_single_type_kv_cache_manager.py -k mamba
pytest tests/v1/core/test_prefix_caching.py -k "external_claim or mamba_align"
```

- `test_mamba_external_claim_admission_matches_allocation` replays the coordinator's order (`add_local_computed_blocks` -> `allocate_external_computed_blocks` -> `allocate_new_blocks`) for a cold prefill and aligned, non-aligned and async claims, each followed by the next chunk, asserting `estimate == allocated`.
- `test_mamba_align_external_claim_admission_matches_allocation` does the same through `KVCacheManager.allocate_slots` on a `full + mamba_align` layout.

Without the fix the sync-claim cases fail (`assert 1 == 2`).

End-to-end: Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 (3 GDN groups) TP1 on H100 with a KV connector doing synchronous loads, `--num-gpu-blocks-override 28 --max-model-len 32768 --max-num-seqs 8`; two 14,012-token prompts whose first 12,544 tokens are served by the connector: prefill cold, `/reset_prefix_cache`, re-send both.

## Test Result

- Without the fix: both warm requests fail, EngineCore exits with the trace above.
- With the fix: both served, 25,088 external tokens loaded per round, repeated twice, no restarts.
- `tests/v1/core/test_single_type_kv_cache_manager.py` + `tests/v1/core/test_prefix_caching.py`: 201 passed on `main` (`a9eafde59c`).

Scheduler admission accounting only; no model outputs affected, no evals run.

title: [Bugfix][HiSparse] Adopt GPU prefix copies after the hit's allocation
body:
## Purpose

Fix an engine crash (`Cannot get N free blocks from the pool`) on a HiSparse host-prefix hit under GPU memory pressure. This is an alternative to #57457.

Closes #59440.

"Adopting" a GPU copy means a host-prefix hit points its page at a still-valid GPU copy of that host page (a GPU-side prefix-cache hit) instead of reading the page back from host.

A host-prefix hit re-pins free GPU copies of its pages so the prefix comes back GPU-resident. Admission counts those copies as free blocks, but adoption pinned them before the hit's own allocation (hot region and new pages), which could then run the pool dry.

#57457 fixes this by charging the pins at admission. That mixes host and GPU accounting in `HiSparseSourceManager.get_num_blocks_to_allocate`, and under pressure it defers a request that could run by reading its prefix from host, just to keep an optimization.

## Changes

HiSparse-only (`vllm/v1/hisparse/coordinator.py`):

- **Adopt after allocation.** `commit_computed_blocks` records the pages to adopt, and `update_residency` (in `cache_blocks`, after `allocate_new_blocks`) adopts the copies that survived. The allocation always gets what admission counted, so no admission accounting is needed. A copy the allocation reuses is dropped by its reuse watcher and never adopted.
- **Tail first.** HiSparse releases a prefix's pages tail first, matching `free_blocks`' convention, so pressure trims a prefix from its end.

Replaying #57457's scenario (a resumed 3-page host prefix hit, `free_blocks` left in the pool):

| `free_blocks` | main | #57457 | this PR |
|---|---|---|---|
| 5–6 | rejected | rejected | rejected |
| 7–8 | crash | rejected | admitted, 0/3 copies |
| 9 | crash | rejected | admitted, 1/3 |
| 10 | 3/3 | 3/3 | 2/3 |
| 11+ | 3/3 | 3/3 | 3/3 |

Near the boundary this keeps fewer copies than #57457, because blocks freed after the copies are queued behind them. #59283, stacked on this PR, is an optional core change that restores 3/3 at 10.

## Test Plan

- `test_hisparse_prefix_hit_under_pressure_adopts_surviving_copies[7, 10]`: exact adopted pages, and no block shared between adopted copies and fresh allocations. `7` fails without the adoption timing, and `10` without tail-first release.
- `tests/v1/core/test_prefix_caching.py` and `tests/v1/core/test_kv_cache_utils.py`, with `CpuPlatform` selected:

```bash
python cpu_pytest.py --confcutdir=tests/v1/core tests/v1/core/test_prefix_caching.py tests/v1/core/test_kv_cache_utils.py
```

## Test Result

- Both new cases fail on main and pass with this PR.
- CPU (`CpuPlatform`): 295 passed. 8 errors are `fixture 'caplog_vllm' not found`, from running outside the top-level conftest, and are identical on main.
- H100, HiSparse unit tests across `tests/v1` (`-k hisparse`): 156 passed.
- H100, `test_prefix_caching.py` + `test_kv_cache_utils.py`: 301 passed. The 2 failures (`test_get_kv_cache_config_mamba_hybrid_sharing_pp_*`) need 4 visible GPUs and fail identically on main with 1.
- H100, `tests/v1/e2e/general/test_hisparse.py`: fails with this PR alone (see the dependency note); with #59235 merged in, 2 passed in each of 2 runs.

title: [V1 Scheduler] Fix Priority Queue Preemption Re-admission (#41951)
body:
Fixes #41951 (supersedes #41952, #56843)

### Why this change is needed

In v1 with `scheduling_policy="priority"`, `PriorityRequestQueue` sorts waiting requests using `Request.__lt__`, which only compared `(priority, arrival_time)`. 

When a running request got preempted due to KV memory pressure, it was pushed back into the heap. If a fresh request with the same priority arrived earlier but hadn't started yet, the heap popped the fresh request first. This left the preempted request sitting idle while incoming requests overwrote its partially computed KV blocks, wasting GPU work and forcing a full recompute once re-admitted.

### What changed

1. **Sort preempted requests ahead of fresh ones (`vllm/v1/request.py`)**:
   Added a `sort_key` property on `Request` and routed `__lt__` through it, boosting preempted requests with `-min(num_preemptions, 3)`. Capping at 3 gives re-admission priority without letting repeatedly preempted requests starve incoming queries.
2. **Anti-thrashing in victim selection (`vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py`)**:
   Updated the preemption victim key to `(r.priority, -min(r.num_preemptions, 3), r.arrival_time)` so the scheduler victimizes least-preempted requests first instead of repeatedly thrashing the same request.
3. Consolidated this fix with @Aravind0403 (who diagnosed the original issue in #41951) and incorporated their unit tests with co-authorship.

This only touches `priority` mode; default FCFS queues and speculative decode paths are unaffected.

### Testing

- `pytest tests/v1/test_request.py -k "test_request_priority_comparison"` (passes)
- `pytest tests/v1/core/test_scheduler.py -k "priority_queue or priority_scheduling_preemption"` (10 passed)
- `ruff check` and `ruff format` clean on modified files.

### AI Usage Disclaimer
The architecture, diagnostic analysis, root-cause investigation, and design choices for this fix are entirely my own. AI tooling was utilized solely as an assistant for refining test case parameterization and code review critique.

title: [Feature]: Cache-aware waiting QoS with optional cooperative prefill preemption
body:
#### Summary

Add an opt-in V1 scheduling policy that improves time-to-first-token (TTFT) for cache-warm continuations under long-context contention:

1. **Cache-aware waiting admission/order**: within a bounded window, prefer a waiting request when its *estimated remaining service cost* is materially lower because a local or external KV prefix is already available.
2. **Optional cooperative prefill preemption (later phase)**: at an ordinary chunked-prefill scheduling boundary, checkpoint and pause a cold running prefill only when doing so is predicted to let a warm request reach its first streamed token significantly sooner, without losing the victim's completed work.

This issue is intended to track one concrete policy/use case. It is compatible with the scheduler extension framework proposed in #51608 rather than a duplicate of that framework.

#### Motivating workload

A single engine may serve many concurrent, long-lived agent sessions with distinct 100k–500k-token histories. Under load, one or more uncached chunked prefills can occupy the running set while a continuation with hundreds of thousands of tokens already present in local APC or an external KV cache remains waiting.

FCFS is fair by arrival time, but it can produce poor interactive latency in this case: the warm continuation may need only a cache transfer, a short uncached suffix, and one decode step, while a cold request ahead of it still has a very large prefill remaining.

This is a QoS/tail-latency proposal, not a claim that cache affinity universally improves throughput. The corrected experiment reported in #42185 found no meaningful benefit for workloads sharing one already-resident prefix; multi-session workloads with distinct competing prefixes are the target case.

#### Residency should be time-aware

A large external-cache hit is not free: the cached prefix must still be loaded into GPU KV and resident while the request runs. However, that occupancy is temporal.

For a warm request, the approximate active residence is:

```
cache load + uncached tail prefill + actual output tokens / effective per-request decode throughput
```

`max_tokens / effective_decode_tokens_per_second` is a useful upper bound for the decode portion (not multiplication); under mixed prefill/decode load, effective per-request decode throughput may be lower. Output KV pages are allocated progressively, while the loaded prompt prefix remains resident until completion or preemption.

The admission objective should therefore consider **KV block-seconds**, not only instantaneous block count or cache-hit percentage. A huge warm prefix with a small output budget can still be an excellent latency trade: large compute avoidance, short expected residence.

#### Phase 1: cache-aware waiting policy

Implement an opt-in policy through #51608's future Score/QueueSort hooks, or initially as a narrowly scoped built-in scheduler policy:

- Preserve explicit request priority as the outer ordering key.
- Inspect only a bounded FCFS/priority-ordered candidate window.
- Use side-effect-free, cycle-cached features.
- Never perform connector RPC or blocking I/O in the scheduler hot path.
- Consider an external hit only after the connector's asynchronous lookup has completed.
- Keep deterministic tie-breaking.

A candidate score should estimate TTFT improvement rather than rank raw hit tokens:

```
warm_ttft_cost =
    ready_cache_transfer_time(tier, bytes)
  + uncached_tokens / observed_prefill_rate
  + first_decode_step_cost

residency_cost =
    required_prompt_blocks * predicted_active_seconds

benefit =
    estimated_head_wait_avoided
  - warm_ttft_cost
  - admission/displacement cost
  - weighted_residency_cost
```

Useful read-only features:

- local cached tokens;
- external cached tokens, lookup readiness, and cache tier;
- estimated transfer bytes/time;
- uncached prompt remainder;
- blocks required for admission;
- prompt-prefill versus active-decode state;
- waiting age, explicit priority, and optional tenant/SLA weight;
- output-token budget as a conservative residence estimate.

The KV connector API may need a side-effect-free snapshot such as:

```python
CacheAdmissionInfo(
    ready: bool,
    matched_tokens: int,
    tier: CacheTier,
    estimated_load_bytes: int,
    estimated_load_seconds: float | None,
)
```

This API must not allocate/touch blocks, emit cache events, increment hit metrics, or start a transfer.

Fairness and anti-thrash controls:

- bounded candidate window;
- maximum FCFS-head wait / aging deadline;
- minimum predicted benefit and hysteresis;
- per-session/tenant bypass budget;
- do not bypass preempted recovery work indefinitely;
- expose decision reasons without high-cardinality metric labels.

#### Phase 2: cooperative cached preemption

Queue reordering alone cannot admit a warm request when running prefixes occupy the required GPU KV. A later opt-in phase could reclaim a running **prefill** at an existing scheduler-step boundary.

Required connector/scheduler contract:

1. Select only a prefill victim; protect active decodes, remote-KV loads, and near-finished prefills.
2. Identify the latest complete cache chunk common to every TP/PP rank.
3. Ensure that prefix is durable and reloadable before freeing its GPU blocks:
   - wait for store completion, or
   - pin the blocks until all-rank completion;
   - do not treat store submission as durability.
4. Requeue the victim with an explicit checkpoint token count.
5. Admit the warm request only if predicted benefit exceeds checkpoint/reload cost.
6. Reload the victim later; recompute only an incomplete tail.
7. On any connector timeout/failure, retain or safely recompute the victim rather than trusting partial external state.

Suggested safeguards:

- cooldown and maximum preemptions per request;
- one cooperative preemption per scheduling cycle;
- no preemption while connector store backlog/failure rate is elevated;
- all-rank acknowledgement and failure injection tests;
- no zero-progress preemption loops;
- request cancellation and repeated-preemption coverage.

#### Observability and evaluation

Split waiting/deferred reasons sufficiently to distinguish cache lookup, KV load, capacity, grammar, and other constraints.

Record:

- candidate local/external hit and tier;
- estimated versus actual load/prefill time;
- scheduler decision reason;
- prompt blocks and predicted/actual block-seconds;
- checkpointed tokens and store-fence latency;
- reload tokens/time and recomputed tail;
- TTFT/time-to-first-stream won or lost;
- preemption count, cooldown rejection, and fairness age.

Acceptance criteria:

- default FCFS and priority behavior is unchanged when disabled;
- scheduler hot path performs no external I/O;
- deterministic unit tests for bounded reorder, aging, explicit priority, and starvation;
- connector tests for delayed/failed all-rank checkpoint and immediate block-ID reuse;
- A/B traces with multiple distinct long-context sessions;
- report scheduler CPU overhead, p50/p95/p99 TTFT, time-to-first-stream, throughput, cache transfer bandwidth, GPU-KV churn, and fairness.

### Alternatives

- **Existing integer priority**: useful for explicit interactive/batch QoS, but it does not estimate cache reuse or residency cost and currently has limited ability to displace running work (#40004, #40087).
- **Smaller prefill chunks / lower `max_num_batched_tokens`**: creates more frequent scheduling boundaries but does not reclaim GPU KV and can reduce aggregate prefill throughput.
- **Session affinity only**: #51384 is a safer and useful local-APC specialization, but external-cache readiness/tier and residency cost remain unmodeled.
- **Residual SJF only**: #51375 captures remaining local work and aging, but does not incorporate external connector transfer cost.
- **External proxy/router**: lacks exact per-engine KV allocation, cache readiness, and preemption state.
- **Whole scheduler subclass**: possible through `scheduler_cls`, but unnecessarily couples a policy experiment to the full scheduler compatibility surface.
- **Separate engines for interactive and batch traffic**: provides isolation but can strand GPU capacity and duplicates large model residency.

### Additional context

Prior art and adjacent work:

- #51608 — extensible scheduler Score/Filter/QueueSort/Preemption hooks.
- #51384 — bounded session-affinity scheduler with local cache confirmation and aging.
- #51375 — residual-aware SJF with aging.
- #42185 — cache-affinity scheduling experiment and workload-dependent result.
- #7883 / #10128 — prefix-cache-aware capacity and token-budget accounting.
- #40004 / #40087 — waiting priority and running-request preemption.
- #31731 / #36390 — KV-heavy head-of-line blocking.
- #30256 — SLA-tiered scheduling.
- LMCache/LMCache#4612 — reload already-cached KV for MP preempted requests.
- vLLM #52360 / #52372 — precedent showing that async stores must not read freed/reused paged-KV blocks.

A staged implementation is important: **waiting-order affinity should land and be measured independently; forced cooperative preemption should remain disabled until durable checkpoint/reload semantics are proven.**

title: [Bug]: Hidden-state extraction inflates KV cache memory requirements by 24× on a hybrid Mamba/MLA model
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

Enabling `extract_hidden_states` with Model Runner V2 on a Kimi-K3 hybrid Mamba/MLA model fails during KV cache initialization.

The hidden-state cache contains one logical layer, but each of its blocks is charged at the width of the largest target-model cache group: 24 layers. This increases its memory contribution from approximately **5.40 GiB to 129.61 GiB**, exceeding available memory.

This is a KV cache admission failure, rather than a CUDA allocation exception.

### Environment

- Model: Kimi-K3, hybrid Mamba/MLA
- Runner: Model Runner V2 (`VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=1`)
- Local vLLM base: `41172e5e47`, with V2 extraction support ported from #49811
- Tensor parallelism: 16
- Extraction dtype: BF16
- Hidden-state connector: custom Mooncake connector
- `max_model_len`: 65536
- `mamba_cache_mode`: `none`

The failure was reproduced on this local branch. It has not been reproduced against an unmodified current upstream checkout.

### Error

```text
ValueError: To serve at least one request with the model's max seq len
(65536), (131.36 GiB KV cache is needed, which is larger than the
available KV cache memory (29.24 GiB).
```

### Diagnostic breakdown

All groups have a physical page size of **442368 bytes**.

| Group | Spec | Layers | Tokens/block | Blocks needed | Admission contribution |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 0 | MambaSpec | 23 | 65536 | 2 | 0.0198 GiB |
| 1 | MambaSpec | 23 | 65536 | 2 | 0.0198 GiB |
| 2 | MambaSpec | 23 | 65536 | 2 | 0.0198 GiB |
| 3 | MLAAttentionSpec | 24 | 384 | 171 | 1.6908 GiB |
| 4 | HiddenStateCacheSpec | 1 | 5 | 13108 | **129.6079 GiB** |

The extraction cache stores six hidden-state vectors per token, each of size 7168:

```text
bytes_per_token = 6 × 7168 × 2 = 86016
tokens_per_page = floor(442368 / 86016) = 5
page_padding = 12288 bytes

hidden-state pages alone:
13108 × 442368 = 5.4003 GiB
```

However, the shared pool uses the maximum group width:

```text
group_size = 24
required_bytes = group_size × page_size × sum(blocks_needed_per_group)
```

Consequently, the singleton extraction group pays for 23 unused layer slots on every block:

```text
hidden-state contribution = 24 × 5.4003 GiB = 129.6079 GiB
total requirement = 131.3580 GiB
```

### Suspected cause

In the affected grouping path:

1. `HiddenStateCacheSpec` is excluded from target-model grouping.
2. The 69 Mamba layers are divided into three groups of 23.
3. The 24 MLA layers form one group.
4. The hidden-state cache is appended as a singleton group, with its page size aligned to the target groups.
5. Both physical allocation and admission accounting use the largest group width.

The shared pool layout therefore introduces substantial unused capacity for the extraction group. Changing only the admission formula would not fix the physical allocation layout.

### Local workaround and observed result

We modified the extraction grouping path to split target groups into singleton groups before appending the hidden-state group:

```python
# vllm/v1/core/kv_cache_utils.py
def get_kv_cache_groups(
    vllm_config: VllmConfig, kv_cache_spec: dict[str, KVCacheSpec]
) -> list[KVCacheGroupSpec]:
    ...
    if hidden_specs:
        groups = [
            replace(group, layer_names=[name])
            for group in groups
            for name in group.layer_names
        ]
    ...
```

This preserves per-layer cache specs and uses the existing shared block pool with one-layer-wide blocks.

Observed diagnostics after the change:

```text
extraction uses single-layer cache groups:
target_groups=4->93 hidden_groups=1

max_model_len=65536
groups=94
max_group_layers=1
available_GiB=29.2441
required_GiB=7.1480
```

The engine successfully starts with extraction enabled.

This validates removal of the admission failure. Extracted hidden-state numerical equivalence and throughput impact have not yet been validated. Singleton grouping increases block-table and scheduler overhead, so it may not be the best general solution.

### Additional comparison

A run without extraction starts with a 2.3298 GiB requirement. However, it has 29 MLA layers and eight blocks per Mamba layer, compared with 24 MLA layers and two blocks in the extraction run. It is therefore not a controlled extraction-only A/B comparison.

### Expected behavior

Adding a singleton hidden-state cache should require storage proportional to its own data, without multiplying that storage by the number of layers in the widest target cache group.

Could the grouping or allocation scheme accommodate this case without requiring one cache group per target layer—for example, through separate pools or a layout that avoids unused layer slots?

### Related

- #49811 — Model Runner V2 support for hidden-state extraction.

title: [Perf][MoE] Support fp8 combine in FlashInfer one-sided MoE all2all
body:
## Purpose
Forwarding fp8 combine flag to increase perf when low precision is supported in FlashInfer combine

## Test Plan
Use GB300 cluster to A/B test with and without the flag `VLLM_FLASHINFER_MOE_A2A_LOW_PRECISION_COMBINE` on, using DeepSeek-R1-0528 NVFP4, 8k input / 1k output.

## Test Result
- For the microbenchmark, there is a small gain at DEP8 (2–8 us per dispatch+combine, about 1–2%), mixed at DEP4. I ran this with just DeepSeek R1 shapes and a sweep across tokens per rank (benchmarks/kernels/benchmark_moe_a2a_combine.py)
- Then I did the serving with nsys (DEP4 and DEP8): the combine kernel is about 17% faster on decode-sized calls but slower on large prefill-sized calls. The fp8 kernel uses 191 registers per thread vs 96 for bf16, could be causing slowdown due to spilling for prefill-sized ones.
- I also tried serving without the profiler, DEP8 (2 nodes); fp8 gave +4.0% output throughput and 2.7% lower median ITL vs bf16. I ran that over 4 server launches (bf16, fp8, fp8, bf16) to balance the order with the benchmark running 3 times each.
- Had a small issue in one of the runs because one of fp8 runs hung shortly after the profiler was stopped. No run hung without the profiler.

Enable flashinfer_nvlink_one_sided backend for all2all by default only for GB200/GB300 with DEP8 or higher topology. title: [ROCm][Perf][DSv4.1] Tune MXFP8 block32 GEMM for DEP8 full-shape projections on MI355X
body:
## Summary

DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash runs attention **data-parallel** at DP8/EP8 (TP=1), so each rank sees the **full (unsharded)** attention + shared-expert projections. Four of these decode shapes were **not** in the `_TUNED` table for `rocm_mxfp8_block32_gemm` and fell through to `_default_config`, which drops to a `128x128x128` tile past M=256 that under-occupies these large-N shapes and roughly **doubles** the per-call cost.

This PR adds tuned tiers for the three shapes that benefit (microbenched per-shape on MI355X, DSpark K6, same method as the existing TP2/TP4 tiers). `shared_down (5120x2304)` was already optimal and is left unchanged. The kernel math is unchanged — only tile selection differs (each candidate was checked to match the baseline output numerically).

## Per-kernel wins (decode M, MI355X)

| Shape | Projection | Win |
|---|---|---|
| `4608 x 5120` | shared gate_up | ~**2.0x** at M≥272 (45→22 µs) |
| `5120 x 8192` | wo_b | ~**1.9x** at M≥272 (61→32 µs); 1.2–1.3x at low M |
| `32768 x 1280` | wq_b | ~**1.4x** at M=224–256 |

## End-to-end (8k/1k, DP8/EP8, MoRI; A/B = these entries on vs off)

| | c256 | c384 |
|---|---|---|
| decode TPOT | −3.9% | −3.8% |
| prefill TTFT | −5.8% | −9.1% |

0 failures over 1k+ requests per side.

## Test plan
- Per-shape microbench vs `_default_config`, with numerical-equality check against the baseline tile.
- End-to-end serving benchmark (8k/1k) at c256/c384, tune on vs off.

title: [Model] Decoder-side SWA bounded replay for DeepSeek-V4.1
body:
## Purpose

Decoder-side SWA bounded replay for DeepSeek-V4.1, on top of the encoder side (#56227). The layers past the last KV-source layer (21-39 of 40 on V4.1-Flash) own only sliding-window KV, so in eager prefill steps they run on each request's last 128 tokens, cold prefills included. Simplified re-submission of #56752 (closed); no other open PR implements this.

- `DeepseekV41ModelState.prepare_attn` prepares the kept rows as a sub-batch, the way a microbatch is prepared: one Triton kernel gathers rows, positions, slot mappings and the replay-layer KV start, and the sub-batch gets attention metadata and a forward context of its own. DP ranks agree on whether any rank trims and on every rank's replay token count.
- `DecoderReplayLayers` gathers the layer inputs by those rows, runs the replay layers under that context and scatters the outputs back.
- Only eager steps trim. A step that fits a CUDA graph (up to 1024 tokens by default) keeps the replay layers on its whole batch inside the graph: such steps are launch-bound, so the graph is worth more than the trim. `prepare_attn` already gets the step's graph mode, which DP ranks share, so there are no nested captures, no eager breaks and no runner changes; the diff is confined to `vllm/models/deepseek_v41/`, a config docstring and the CI job list.
- With the fused MoE finalize of #58586, a decode step's cut layer hands its unfinalized `MoEOutput` to the replay layers unchanged, and layer 21's first boundary finalizes it. A trimming step holds a prefill longer than the window, more tokens than any step that defers its finalize, so the trim path only sees tensors.
- Stays off, with a warning, when the PP stage does not hold every layer after the cut, under sequence-parallel MoE, PCP or microbatching, with an Engram layer after the cut, or with a drafter window wider than the target's. `--no-swa-bounded-replay` turns off both sides. A no-op on ROCm.

## Test Plan

```
pytest tests/models/test_deepseek_v41_replay_batch.py tests/models/test_deepseek_v41_decoder_replay_layers.py
```

- Accuracy: gsm8k 5-shot, n=1319, two passes against one server (pass 2 is all full-prompt prefix hits).
- Performance: `vllm-bench`, random token-id prompts, prefix cache reset before every point.
- Both on V4.1-Flash, TP4 and DP4 x TP1 x EP4 (DEP4), decoder side on vs off with the encoder side on in both (off via a local patch, not in this PR).

## Test Result

Unit tests cover the replay rows and sub-batch metadata (adaptive verification, prompt-logprobs requests, DP agreement), graph steps getting no replay batch, and the gather/scatter with the indexer buffers. pre-commit and mypy are clean.

### Accuracy (GB200, V4.1-Flash)

| arm | pass 1 (cold) | pass 2 (prefix hits) |
|---|---|---|
| TP4, decoder replay on | 0.9249 | 0.9234 |
| TP4, decoder replay off | 0.9303 | 0.9249 |
| DEP4, decoder replay on | 0.9333 | 0.9287 |
| DEP4, decoder replay off | 0.9257 | 0.9181 |

`exact_match/flexible-extract`; one standard error is 0.0072. 0 request errors. On TP4 the fused MoE finalize of #58586 is active, so every decode step passes the cut layer's unfinalized MoE output through the replay layers.

### Performance (GB200, V4.1-Flash)

Saturated prefill throughput with decoder replay stays at 83K-86K tok/s on TP4 and 199K-228K on DEP4 at every prompt length, against 68K-54K and 134K-120K without. From 16K up, prefill TTFT drops 25-36% on TP4 and 37-45% on DEP4 at any concurrency, and TPOT drops up to 29% and 39% at high concurrency.

TP4:

|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1K | 209 / 197 ms | 256 | 198.6K / 132.0K (+50%) | +4% | -1% |

Those steps are launch-bound (~175 ms of kernel launches with the GPU waiting on the CPU), so the trim saves no time there. A no-op: the ROCm model classes have no `decoder_replay_layers`, and the encoder side stays off on ROCm as before. The new tests are not in the AMD mirror of the CI job. title: [Perf][DSv4.1] Exchange packed FP8 Engram rows across DP and feed wkv MXFP8
body:
## Purpose

DeepSeek-V4.1's Engram tables are already MXFP8 (FP8 rows with one ue8m0 scale per 32 values) and `wkv` is an MXFP8 GEMM, but the lookup dequantizes each row to BF16, DP replicas all-gather those 512-byte rows layer by layer, and `wkv` quantizes them right back. This PR keeps rows packed from the host table to `wkv`.

- **Packed rows, direct MXFP8.** The lookup copies each row's 256 FP8 bytes and 8 scale bytes as they are, and one unpack kernel writes them in FlashInfer's MXFP8 activation layout (F8_128x4 scales). `wkv` takes them as a `QuantizedActivation`, so both the dequant and the requant are gone, and the output is bit-identical.
- **One all-to-all per prefill step.** `EngramBatch` looks up every local Engram layer into one packed buffer and exchanges it with a single all-to-all, which sends each rank only its own tokens (264 instead of 512 bytes per head row, 1/DP of an all-gather), then unpacks all layers in one launch.
- **Peer exchange for decode.** Below 128 tokens per rank, `EngramPeerExchange` replaces the hash all-gather and the per-layer row all-gathers: ranks publish ids in symmetric memory, look up their head shard for every peer's tokens, and read their own tokens back from the peers after a barrier. All layers share one lookup and one unpack launch.

The batched path serves DP-sharded tables (`embedding_across_dp` without DP-shared memory) with TP = 1, `head_dim % 128 == 0`, no LoRA (it wraps `wkv` after construction), and a `wkv` kernel that takes F8_128x4 scales (reusing `can_fuse_query_quant`). The peer exchange also needs SM100, CPU offload, and 2/4/8 fully connected GPUs; without it every slot uses the all-to-all, which on DEP4 HBM tables at 1–127 tokens per rank is 19–58 us faster than the BF16 path. Everything else, including TP, DP-shared tables, single replicas and ROCm, keeps the existing BF16 path unchanged. Communication stays on the current stream and `wkv` still runs in `Engram.forward`.

Also changed along the way:

- `EngramBatch` is an `nn.Module`, so the peer exchange's pointer tables are model buffers that level-2 sleep restores.
- `fused_q_kv_rmsnorm_quant` and the Engram unpack kernel share the F8_128x4 scale offset and size helpers.

## Kernel microbenchmark

The benchmarks, E2E runs and the first accuracy table were measured on d593d7f5df. 3724967bb9 only drops paths that DEP + THP never takes and keeps its `wkv` outputs bitwise identical (see Test Result).

Engram only, two layers (lookup, exchange, and anything needed to reach the MXFP8 `wkv` input), 4 x GB300 in one node. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash table sizes (24 heads x 16M rows, 94.4 GiB per layer) as DP-shared `/dev/shm` tables or private THP shards, uniform random ids rotating 3 sets, 256 MiB L2 flush per sample, full CUDA graph replay, median of 40 samples of the slowest rank, best of 2 rounds. Since this PR's output is already the `wkv` input, the BF16 columns include their activation quantization (17 us for decode, 203 us at 32K tokens).

DEP4:

| tokens/rank | DP-shared (us) | THP + all-gather (us) | this PR (us) | vs THP + all-gather |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 34 | 80 | 36 | 2.22x |
| 8 | 34 | 81 | 38 | 2.13x |
| 32 | 38 | 93 | 40 | 2.33x |
| 64 | 44 | 106 | 43 | 2.47x |
| 127 | 136 | 136 | 50 | 2.72x |
| 128 | 140 | 136 | 72 | 1.89x |
| 1024 | 2442 | 315 | 179 | 1.76x |
| 4096 | 5326 | 1097 | 534 | 2.05x |
| 8192 | 8224 | 2087 | 1010 | 2.07x |
| 16384 | 11854 | 4047 | 1954 | 2.07x |
| 32768 | 16008 | 7860 | 3800 | 2.07x |

DEP2:

| tokens/rank | DP-shared (us) | THP + all-gather (us) | this PR (us) | vs THP + all-gather |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 34 | 73 | 38 | 1.92x |
| 8 | 34 | 74 | 40 | 1.85x |
| 32 | 35 | 81 | 43 | 1.88x |
| 64 | 41 | 90 | 44 | 2.05x |
| 127 | 66 | 107 | 49 | 2.18x |
| 128 | 62 | 107 | 71 | 1.51x |
| 1024 | 2015 | 228 | 168 | 1.36x |
| 4096 | 4629 | 754 | 507 | 1.49x |
| 8192 | 6873 | 1407 | 970 | 1.45x |
| 16384 | 9511 | 2709 | 1879 | 1.44x |
| 32768 | 12389 | 5268 | 3672 | 1.43x |

DP-shared tables need no exchange, so at 1–64 tokens they are at most 8 us faster than this PR; from 1024 tokens this PR is 3.4–13.6x faster than them. The 127 → 128 step is the switch from the peer exchange to the all-to-all.

## Test Plan

```bash
pytest tests/kernels/test_engram.py tests/distributed/test_engram_dp_shard.py tests/kernels/core/test_fused_q_kv_rmsnorm.py -q
pre-commit run --files <changed files>
pre-commit run mypy-3.12 --files <changed files> --hook-stage manual
```

New coverage: the packed lookup output, and a 4-GPU check of the batched staging across peer and all-to-all slots, uneven and idle replicas, and full and breakable CUDA graph replays. The peer path needs SM100, so other GPUs only cover the all-to-all path.

## Test Result

On 3724967bb9, 202 passed on 4x GB200 (102 Engram kernel, 27 distributed, 73 `test_fused_q_kv_rmsnorm.py`). Ruff, format and mypy pass.

Also checked locally, without adding tests:

- The staged MXFP8 bytes equal the table rows byte for byte on DEP2 and DEP4 with 22 and 24 heads, 1–3 layers starting at a non-zero hash index, pinned, THP and HBM tables, 1–4096 tokens around the 127/128 boundary (sorted lookups included), and 24 unsynchronized steps that switch between peer exchange and all-to-all.
- Real layer 1 and 14 checkpoint rows and `wkv` weights: the `wkv` output is bitwise identical to the BF16 path at 129, 1024 and 4096 tokens, with CuTe-DSL and CUTLASS.
- DEP4 `Engram.forward` through the peer exchange and the all-to-all in eager mode and full and breakable graph replays: bitwise identical to the BF16 path.
- 3724967bb9 vs d593d7f5df on DEP4 (24 heads x 256, 2 layers, 10% dead ids, idle ranks; pinned tables at 1–512 and HBM tables at 128–512 tokens per rank): staged MXFP8 values and `wkv` outputs (CuTe-DSL and CUTLASS) are bitwise identical; only the scales of padding and unowned rows change from 127 to 0.
- After a simulated level-2 sleep the peer exchange's pointer tables are restored and its lookups stay exact.

## E2E prefill (DEP4)

DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, DEP4 (DP4 x TP1 + EP) on one GB300 node: DeepGEMM mega MoE, FlashInfer sparse MLA, fp8 KV cache, `max_num_batched_tokens=16384`, prefix caching off. Offline `LLM` per DP rank, one prompt per rank (nominal length minus 7 tokens per rank), `max_tokens=1`; TTFT is `scheduled_ts` to `first_token_ts` on the slowest rank, median of 3 repeats after a warmup repeat. Measured on top of #59532 with `max_cudagraph_capture_size=8192` (default size list, so 1K–8K prefills run in PIECEWISE graphs) and `max_num_seqs=64`. Prompts are uniformly random token ids; a repeated sentence keeps the few distinct n-gram rows in cache and hides Engram entirely.

| tokens/rank | DP-shared TTFT (ms) | THP + all-gather TTFT (ms) | this PR TTFT (ms) | vs DP-shared | vs THP + all-gather |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1024 | 60.2 | 61.7 | 60.5 | 0.99x | 1.02x |
| 4096 | 129.7 | 128.0 | 127.2 | 1.02x | 1.01x |
| 8192 | 220.2 | 214.2 | 213.9 | 1.03x | 1.00x |
| 16384 | 248.1 | 242.6 | 240.5 | 1.03x | 1.01x |
| 32768 | 466.0 | 447.4 | 446.5 | 1.04x | 1.00x |

Repeat spread is under 2.5 ms (5 ms for DP-shared at 32K). The gain over DP-shared tables matches the microbenchmark: at 8K the two Engram layers take 7.2 ms less, close to the 6.3 ms measured end to end. Against THP tables with all-gather it is about 1 ms per step, within noise end to end.

## E2E decode (DEP4)

Same setup on `main` (default capture sizes up to 512, `max_num_seqs=128`), short prompts, 64 output tokens with the decode token fixed to hold MoE routing constant. Mean request TPOT of the slowest rank, median of 3 repeats after a warmup repeat.

| batch/rank | DP-shared TPOT (ms) | THP + all-gather TPOT (ms) | this PR TPOT (ms) | vs DP-shared | vs THP + all-gather |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 6.072 | 6.128 | 6.082 | 1.00x | 1.01x |
| 8 | 6.457 | 6.501 | 6.453 | 1.00x | 1.01x |
| 32 | 8.199 | 8.292 | 7.928 | 1.03x | 1.05x |
| 64 | 10.833 | 11.157 | 10.832 | 1.00x | 1.03x |
| 127 | 14.043 | 14.403 | 14.046 | 1.00x | 1.03x |

Engram is under 1% of TPOT, and the fixed decode token keeps its rows cache-resident, so decode shows that private THP tables no longer cost anything over DP-shared ones rather than the full lookup saving.

## Accuracy (DEP4, this PR)

GSM8K with lm-eval 0.4.13: 1319 problems, 5-shot completions, temperature 0, 4096-token cap, concurrency 32, two passes on one `vllm serve` DEP4 server per side (same engine setup as the E2E runs, `main` with DP-shared tables vs this PR with THP tables). No request errors.

| | strict match (pass 1 / 2) | flexible extract (pass 1 / 2) |
|---|---|---|
| `main`, DP-shared tables | 92.87% / 92.95% | 92.80% / 92.87% |
| this PR, THP tables | 93.33% / 93.10% | 93.25% / 93.03% |

Both are within one standard error (±0.7 points); no accuracy gain is claimed.

GSM8K with DSpark on 3724967bb9 (DEP4, MegaMoE, `FLASHMLA_MEGA_ATTN_DSV41`, 5 speculative tokens with adaptive verification, THP tables; same lm-eval setup with a 1024-token cap), against the DEP4 base run in #59511 with DP-shared tables:

| | strict match | acceptance length, incl. bonus | per-position acceptance |
|---|---|---|---|
| #59511 base, DP-shared tables | 92.57% | 3.365 | 0.792 / 0.641 / 0.441 / 0.310 / 0.181 |
| this PR, THP tables | 92.57% | 3.398 | 0.795 / 0.644 / 0.446 / 0.319 / 0.194 |

<details>
<summary>Commands</summary>

```bash
vllm serve <model> --served-model-name DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash \
  --data-parallel-size 4 --enable-expert-parallel --tokenizer-mode deepseek_v41 \
  --language-model-only --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 \
  --max-num-seqs 256 --max-num-batched-tokens 16384 --max-model-len 32768 \
  --attention-config '{"backend":"FLASHINFER_MLA_SPARSE_DSV41","indexer_kv_dtype":"mxfp4","indexer_sparse_logits":true}' \
  --kernel-config '{"moe_backend":"deep_gemm_mega_moe"}' \
  --kv-cache-dtype fp8 --no-enable-prefix-caching \
  --engram-config '{"cpu_offload":true,"embedding_across_dp":true,"dp_shared_memory":false,"use_thp":true}'

lm_eval --model local-completions \
  --model_args "model=DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash,base_url=http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/completions,num_concurrent=32,max_retries=3,tokenized_requests=False,tokenizer_backend=None" \
  --tasks gsm8k --num_fewshot 5 --gen_kwargs "max_gen_toks=4096,temperature=0"
```

The baseline uses `"dp_shared_memory":true,"use_thp":false`. The DSpark run uses the DEP4 GSM8K serve flags from #59511 plus the `--engram-config` above, and `max_gen_toks=1024`.

</details>

## Not a duplicate

Searched open PRs for `engram`, `engram fp8`, `engram all-to-all`, `engram peer` and `DeepSeek-V4.1 engram`. #56989 packs FP8 rows for the TP head exchange (opt-in, TP > 1 without SP) and dequantizes them before `wkv`; this PR leaves TP alone and covers Engram DP, feeding `wkv` directly. #57893 tunes small-lookup tiles. #58766 fed MXFP8 rows to `wkv` through the existing gathers and was closed by its author after merge conflicts, without review; this PR keeps that idea and also replaces the gathers.

title: [RFC]: Per-instance EPLB metrics
body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

(co-authored with @sallyom and Claude)

In replicated vLLM deployments behind a load balancer, the load balancer has no visibility into EPLB (Expert-Parallel Load Balancing) state when making routing decisions. EPLB dynamically replicates heavily-used experts across EP ranks to balance load, and instances experiencing high expert load imbalance or active rebalancing operations have degraded capacity. Without metrics exposing this state, load balancers cannot avoid routing traffic to struggling instances, leading to suboptimal performance and increased tail latencies.

EPLB already tracks and logs this information to stdout when `--eplb-log-balancedness` is enabled:

```
EPLB step: 2500: avg_tokens=1024, max_tokens=2048, balancedness=0.5000
```

But these are obviously not queryable by load balancers. This proposal exports the same data that's currently logged as Prometheus metrics, enabling intelligent load balancing decisions based on instance health.

Note - these stats are EP-group-wide, and should not be reported per-engine (i.e. with the `engine_idx` label), instead they should probably only be recorded on DP rank 0.

## Proposed Metrics

| Metric Name | Type | Description
|-------------|------|-------------|
| `vllm:eplb_avg_tokens_per_rank` | Gauge | Average tokens per EP rank in current interval |
| `vllm:eplb_max_tokens_per_rank` | Gauge | Maximum tokens across EP ranks in current interval |
| `vllm:eplb_rebalancing` | Gauge | Whether EPLB is currently rebalancing (0 or 1) |
| `vllm:eplb_rebalance_events_total` | Counter | Total number of EPLB rebalancing operations |

## Sample PromQL

```promql
# Imbalance ratio - 0.5 means 50% balanced
(vllm:eplb_avg_tokens_per_rank / vllm:eplb_max_tokens_per_rank)

# Relative imbalance: avoid instances where one rank is 2x overloaded
(vllm:eplb_max_tokens_per_rank / vllm:eplb_avg_tokens_per_rank) > 2.0

# Absolute imbalance: avoid instances with severe token gap
(vllm:eplb_max_tokens_per_rank - vllm:eplb_avg_tokens_per_rank) > 5000

# Hybrid: high load AND poor balance (most dangerous)
vllm:eplb_max_tokens_per_rank > 15000
AND (vllm:eplb_max_tokens_per_rank / vllm:eplb_avg_tokens_per_rank) > 1.5

# Alert on thrashing
rate(vllm:eplb_rebalance_events_total[5m]) > 2

# Reduce traffic to instance currently rebalancing
vllm:eplb_rebalancing == 1
```

### Alternatives

_No response_

### Additional context

_No response_

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [Docs] Document engine-aware routing with vLLM Router for DP deployments
body:
Add a section to data_parallel_deployment.md explaining how vLLM Router's --intra-node-data-parallel-size flag combined with the consistent_hash policy enables session-affinity routing to individual DP engines within a single endpoint, useful for conversational/agentic workloads that benefit from prefix-cache reuse.

Closes #58160




## Purpose

Fixes #58160

The `data_parallel_deployment.md` page documents three ways to load-balance
requests across DP ranks (Internal, Hybrid, External), but doesn't mention
that [vLLM Router](https://github.com/vllm-project/router) can route
requests to *individual* DP engines within a deployment via
`--intra-node-data-parallel-size N`, combined with the `consistent_hash`
policy for session-affinity routing.

This is particularly useful for conversational/agentic workloads, where
pinning a session's follow-up requests to the same DP engine lets that
engine reuse its prefix/KV cache instead of recomputing it each turn.

As noted in the issue, this capability doesn't cleanly fit the existing
Internal/Hybrid/External classification, since it's an external tool that
is topology-aware rather than treating each endpoint as opaque. This PR
adds a new section, "Engine-Aware Routing with vLLM Router," after the
External Load Balancing section, with an example that composes it with
Hybrid Load Balancing.


## Test Plan

This is a documentation-only change (no code paths affected). Validated with:

- `pre-commit run markdownlint-cli2 --files docs/serving/data_parallel_deployment.md`
- Manual review of the rendered Markdown, including verifying the
  `#hybrid-load-balancing` anchor link and all external links resolve
  correctly.

## Test Result

`markdownlint-cli2` passed with no errors or warnings on the modified file.

title: [Docs] Document DP-aware routing with vLLM Router in the DP deployment guide
body:
## Purpose

`serving/data_parallel_deployment.md` only describes internal, hybrid and external load balancing. It does not mention that the vLLM Router can front a single DP endpoint and route requests to individual DP ranks, which enables session-affinity routing for conversational/agentic workloads.

Add a short "DP-aware routing with vLLM Router" section:

- explain `--intra-node-data-parallel-size N` (the number of internal DP ranks behind each worker URL; DP-aware routing is enabled automatically when `N > 1`);
- note the `X-data-parallel-rank` header that the vLLM API server dispatches on;
- show how pairing it with `--policy consistent_hash` pins a session to one rank so its prefix/KV cache is reused;

Addresses #58160.
