title: [Bugfix][Metrics] Retain components for resolved quantization configs
body:
## Overview

Fixes #58742. Resolved quantization names missing from the estimator lookup silently drop attention and FFN work from MFU/MBU estimates.

## Claims

- Resolve weight size from GPTQ/AWQ bit widths, online quantization specifications, and mixed linear/expert precision.
- Retain components with a deduplicated warning and model-dtype estimate when an unsupported method or checkpoint layer selection cannot be represented by one width.
- Preserve existing supported methods and unquantized controls.

## Validation

Rebased onto current main `276fbcf`, resolving the upstream move of `Self` into `typing`. Implementation and test bodies are unchanged from the previously tested branch.

```bash
OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 .venv/bin/python -m pytest --confcutdir=tests/v1/metrics tests/v1/metrics/test_perf_metrics.py -q
.venv/bin/pre-commit run --files vllm/v1/metrics/perf.py tests/v1/metrics/test_perf_metrics.py
```

**100 metrics tests passed.** All applicable pre-commit checks passed, including the repository's minimum-version mypy check.

Executed 16 real checkpoint/flag combinations six times against the rebased stack: **96 online runs passed**, each evaluating prefill and decode. A separate 16-case run used the unpatched current-main estimator with identical checkpoint revisions, configuration hashes, and resolved layer lists. All repeats were identical; unaffected controls and the previously approved estimates were unchanged.

| Checkpoint | Upstream decode GFLOPs | Patched decode GFLOPs |
|---|---:|---:|
| GPT-OSS-20B | 1.158 | 7.436 |
| Qwen2.5 GPTQ/AWQ | 0.272 | 1.076 |
| Qwen3 bf16 control | 1.427 | 1.427 |

Validation used Python 3.12 and CPU Torch with actual `ModelConfig`, `VllmConfig._get_quantization_config`, and estimator execution. No weights were loaded or GPU inference run; model outputs, kernels, and serving behavior are unchanged.

## Details

Both attention and FFN parsers share weight-size resolution. GPT-OSS retains bf16 linear layers and FP4 expert accounting; DeepSeek-V4's FFN accounting is restored while its separate unsupported attention architecture remains outside this fix.

The fallback can overestimate weight traffic and does not provide per-layer accounting. Automatically discovered layer lists in the tested Qwen GPTQ/AWQ checkpoints trigger the documented 2-byte fallback rather than assuming every projection is 4-bit.

No overlapping fix was found in issue-number or area searches. Related #58745, #58836, and #54228 address speculative-token accounting, hybrid attention, and expert activation counts respectively.

<details>
<summary>Pull Request Checklist</summary>

- [x] Design Fit: confines changes to the analytic estimator and shares resolution between its parsers.
- [x] Testing and Validation: regression coverage and real configuration execution passed; upstream CI remains maintainer-authorized.
- [x] Code Quality and Style: current pre-commit and type checks passed.
- [x] Pull Request Contents: issue, reproducer commands, results, and limitations are included.

</details>

title: [Feature]: Recency-based progressive mixed-precision KV cache
body:
## The feature, motivation and pitch

## Summary

I would like to propose a generic recency-based progressive mixed-precision KV cache.

Instead of storing the entire KV cache using one uniform format, vLLM would keep recently created KV blocks in a user-selected higher-precision tier and progressively quantize older completed blocks into lower-precision tiers.

The feature should **not be hardcoded to BF16 as the highest tier**. The ordered precision policy should be configurable. Examples include:

```text
BF16 -> FP8
BF16 -> FP8 -> NVFP4
BF16 -> NVFP4
FP8 -> NVFP4
NVFP4 -> a future lower-precision format
```

Example percentage-based policies:

```text
newest 20%: BF16
next 20%: FP8 E4M3
oldest 60%: NVFP4
```

or, for a cache whose highest selected precision is FP8:

```text
newest 20%: FP8 E4M3
oldest 80%: NVFP4
```

New KV entries and the active partially filled tail block would be written into the **first/highest tier selected by the policy**, which may be BF16, FP8, NVFP4, or another supported format. Once a block is complete and crosses a configured age boundary, it could be asynchronously quantized and moved to the next lower-precision pool.

This proposal is specifically about using different KV-cache formats **within the same attention layer based on block age**. It is different from layer-wise mixed precision, where different transformer layers use different formats.

## Motivation

Long-context KV caches consume a substantial amount of GPU memory. A uniform low-precision KV cache reduces memory usage, but it applies the same precision to recent and old entries.

For long-context and agentic workloads, it may be useful to preserve a recent window in the policy's selected highest precision while compressing older context more aggressively.

The intended abstraction is not a single special-case mode such as BF16 + FP8 + NVFP4. It is a generic ordered list of storage tiers. For example:

- a BF16-based policy can progressively demote blocks into FP8 and NVFP4;
- an FP8-based policy can progressively demote blocks into NVFP4;
- an NVFP4-based policy could use a future lower-precision storage format when one is supported;
- different hardware backends may expose different valid tier combinations.

This should be treated as a hypothesis that needs quality and performance benchmarking rather than an assumption that recent tokens are always more important.

## Example memory calculation

The following example uses a Llama-3.1-70B-style GQA configuration:

- context length: 64,000 tokens
- number of layers: 80
- KV heads: 8
- head dimension: 128
- both K and V are stored
- one fully populated sequence
- values are aggregated across all tensor-parallel ranks

The number of stored scalar values is:

```text
64,000 tokens × 80 layers × 2 (K and V) × 8 KV heads × 128 dimensions
= 10,485,760,000 values
```

The generic calculation for a progressive policy is:

```text
effective bits/value = sum(tier_fraction × tier_effective_bits)

KV-cache size =
    number_of_values × effective_bits_per_value / 8
```

For NVFP4, the estimates below assume packed 4-bit data and one FP8 block scale per 16 values, or approximately 4.5 effective bits per value. FP8 is approximated as 8 bits per value. Small allocator, alignment, block-table, tensor-scale, and kernel-workspace overheads are not included.

### Absolute VRAM comparison

| KV-cache policy | Effective bits/value | Total KV cache | Per GPU with TP=8 | Saving vs uniform BF16 | Capacity vs uniform BF16 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Uniform BF16 | 16.0 | 19.53 GiB | 2.44 GiB | 0.00% | 1.00x |
| Progressive: 20% BF16 + 80% FP8 | 9.6 | 11.72 GiB | 1.46 GiB | 40.00% | 1.67x |
| Uniform FP8 | 8.0 | 9.77 GiB | 1.22 GiB | 50.00% | 2.00x |
| Progressive: 20% BF16 + 20% FP8 + 60% NVFP4 | 7.5 | 9.16 GiB | 1.14 GiB | 53.13% | 2.13x |
| Progressive: 20% BF16 + 80% NVFP4 | 6.8 | 8.30 GiB | 1.04 GiB | 57.50% | 2.35x |
| Progressive: 20% FP8 + 80% NVFP4 | 5.2 | 6.35 GiB | 0.79 GiB | 67.50% | 3.08x |
| Uniform NVFP4 | ~4.5 | 5.49 GiB | 0.69 GiB | 71.88% | 3.56x |

### Correct baseline for each progressive policy

A progressive policy should be compared with a uniform cache using the policy's own highest selected precision.

| Progressive policy | Uniform reference | Progressive KV size | Uniform reference size | Saving vs its own reference | Capacity vs its own reference |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 20% BF16 + 80% FP8 | Uniform BF16 | 11.72 GiB | 19.53 GiB | 40.00% | 1.67x |
| 20% BF16 + 20% FP8 + 60% NVFP4 | Uniform BF16 | 9.16 GiB | 19.53 GiB | 53.13% | 2.13x |
| 20% BF16 + 80% NVFP4 | Uniform BF16 | 8.30 GiB | 19.53 GiB | 57.50% | 2.35x |
| 20% FP8 + 80% NVFP4 | Uniform FP8 | 6.35 GiB | 9.77 GiB | 35.00% | 1.54x |

This distinction is important:

- `BF16 -> FP8 -> NVFP4` is a BF16-based progressive policy and should primarily be compared with uniform BF16.
- `FP8 -> NVFP4` is an FP8-based progressive policy and should primarily be compared with uniform FP8.
- Uniform FP8 is therefore not merely a competing alternative to one BF16-based progressive mode; it can itself be the highest tier of another progressive policy.
- Uniform NVFP4 is the lowest uniform format in this example. The same abstraction should extend below NVFP4 when a supported lower-precision format becomes available.

### Breakdown: BF16 -> FP8 -> NVFP4

Policy:

```text
newest 20%: BF16
next 20%: FP8
oldest 60%: NVFP4
```

| Tier | Tokens | Format | Estimated memory |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Recent/hot | 12,800 | BF16 | 3.91 GiB |
| Intermediate/warm | 12,800 | FP8 | 1.95 GiB |
| Old/cold | 38,400 | NVFP4 | 3.30 GiB |
| **Total** | **64,000** | Mixed | **9.16 GiB** |

Compared with uniform BF16, this policy saves approximately **10.38 GiB**, or **53.13%**, per 64K sequence.

### Breakdown: FP8 -> NVFP4

Policy:

```text
newest 20%: FP8
oldest 80%: NVFP4
```

| Tier | Tokens | Format | Estimated memory |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Recent/hot | 12,800 | FP8 | 1.95 GiB |
| Old/cold | 51,200 | NVFP4 | 4.39 GiB |
| **Total** | **64,000** | Mixed | **6.35 GiB** |

Compared with uniform FP8, this policy saves approximately **3.42 GiB**, or **35.00%**, per 64K sequence.

This is the appropriate FP8-level comparison. It demonstrates that recency-based progression can be applied even when the selected hot tier is already quantized.

## Possible user-facing configuration

The configuration should accept an arbitrary ordered list of supported tiers rather than enabling one hardcoded BF16-based layout.

Percentage-based policies:

```bash
--kv-cache-dtype-policy "bf16:20%,fp8_e4m3:20%,nvfp4:60%"
```

```bash
--kv-cache-dtype-policy "fp8_e4m3:20%,nvfp4:80%"
```

```bash
--kv-cache-dtype-policy "bf16:20%,nvfp4:80%"
```

An absolute-window policy may be easier to provision in production:

```bash
--kv-cache-dtype-policy \
  "bf16:last=4096,fp8_e4m3:last=12288,nvfp4:rest"
```

or:

```bash
--kv-cache-dtype-policy \
  "fp8_e4m3:last=4096,nvfp4:rest"
```

The exact CLI and configuration format are open for discussion. The key requirement is that the first tier must not be implicitly fixed to BF16.

## Possible implementation direction

PagedAttention already manages KV data in blocks, so the feature could be implemented using multiple physical page pools selected by the configured policy.

For example:

```text
Policy A:
BF16 hot pool
FP8 warm pool
NVFP4 cold pool

Policy B:
FP8 hot pool
NVFP4 cold pool
```

A logical KV block ID could map to a physical location:

```text
logical_block_id -> (tier_id, physical_page_id)
```

The lifecycle would be:

1. Allocate and write new KV blocks in the policy's first/highest tier.
2. Keep partially filled blocks in that tier.
3. When a completed block becomes old enough, allocate a page in the next configured tier.
4. Quantize/copy the block asynchronously.
5. Atomically update its logical-to-physical mapping.
6. Release the source page after the migration completes.
7. Never promote a quantized block to a higher precision unless an original higher-precision copy is still available.

Each block would normally move only in one direction through the configured tier list:

```text
tier[0] -> tier[1] -> ... -> tier[n - 1]
```

Concrete examples:

```text
BF16 -> FP8 -> NVFP4
FP8 -> NVFP4
BF16 -> NVFP4
```

Attention could initially be implemented as one attention operation per non-empty tier, followed by an LSE-aware merge of the partial attention states. A later optimized implementation could process all contiguous age segments in one mixed-tier online-softmax kernel.

## Suggested MVP

A smaller first implementation could support:

- a generic two-tier policy;
- an absolute recent window;
- completed-block demotion only;
- Triton attention backend only;
- decode workloads;
- no prefix caching;
- no speculative decoding.

The first validated pair could be:

```text
newest 4,096 tokens: BF16
all older tokens: FP8 E4M3
```

The abstraction should not assume that this is the only valid pair. A subsequent backend-supported policy could be:

```text
newest 4,096 tokens: FP8 E4M3
all older tokens: NVFP4
```

This would allow the project to measure:

1. quality relative to the corresponding uniform highest-tier format;
2. quantization and migration overhead;
3. decode latency and memory-bandwidth changes;
4. scheduler and allocator complexity;
5. whether multi-pass attention is fast enough before implementing a fused kernel;
6. whether the same abstraction works correctly for both BF16-based and FP8-based policies.

## Important design questions

### Supported precision graph

The cache policy should be validated against backend-supported conversions.

Examples may include:

```text
BF16 -> FP8
BF16 -> NVFP4
FP8 -> NVFP4
BF16 -> FP8 -> NVFP4
```

The core interface should remain generic enough for future lower-precision formats, while each attention backend advertises the tier combinations and conversion paths it actually supports.

### Prefix caching

A shared prefix block can have different logical ages for different requests. For an MVP, progressive quantization could be declared incompatible with prefix caching.

Possible later policies include:

- shared prefix blocks are always stored in the lowest configured tier;
- copy-on-write when a request requires a different precision;
- store precision as a property of the physical shared block rather than each request.

### Pool sizing and scheduling

The scheduler would need to account for capacity separately for each configured tier.

When a higher-precision pool is full, it could first demote eligible blocks into the next configured tier. If that tier is full, the scheduler could continue cascading demotions through the policy before preempting a request.

This logic should operate over a generic ordered tier list rather than hardcoded BF16, FP8, and NVFP4 pool names.

### Block boundaries

Precision transitions should happen only at KV block boundaries. Requested percentages or token windows therefore need to be rounded according to the configured block size.

### Backend support

The supported tier combinations would depend on attention backend and hardware capabilities. A backend may initially expose only BF16 + FP8, while another may also support FP8 + NVFP4 or BF16 + FP8 + NVFP4.

### Accuracy evaluation

Each progressive policy should be benchmarked against its corresponding uniform highest-tier cache.

Useful comparisons include:

- uniform BF16 vs BF16 -> FP8;
- uniform BF16 vs BF16 -> FP8 -> NVFP4;
- uniform BF16 vs BF16 -> NVFP4;
- uniform FP8 vs FP8 -> NVFP4;
- uniform NVFP4 vs future NVFP4-based lower-precision policies;
- multiple recent-window sizes;
- percentage-based versus fixed-size windows.

Possible metrics include perplexity, long-context retrieval accuracy, task accuracy, TTFT, ITL, throughput, migration bandwidth, and peak KV-cache memory.

## Expected behavior when disabled

The feature should be opt-in. Existing uniform KV-cache configurations and their allocation, scheduling, and kernel paths should remain unchanged when no progressive policy is configured.

---

## Alternatives

### Uniform single-format KV cache

Uniform BF16, FP8, or NVFP4 cache is simpler to allocate and execute, but it uses the same format for every token regardless of age.

Each of these formats should also be considered a possible highest or lowest tier in a progressive policy rather than only as an alternative to the feature.

For example:

```text
uniform BF16 reference -> progressive BF16 + FP8 or BF16 + FP8 + NVFP4
uniform FP8 reference  -> progressive FP8 + NVFP4
uniform NVFP4 reference -> future progressive NVFP4 + lower format
```

### Layer-wise mixed precision

Related to #22195.

Layer-wise mixed precision assigns formats based on transformer layer sensitivity. This is complementary to the proposed feature: recency-based quantization assigns formats based on the age of blocks within each layer.

Both approaches could eventually be combined, but supporting both dimensions in an initial implementation would substantially increase allocator and kernel complexity.

### Sparse KV-cache eviction

Related to #5751.

Sparse eviction reduces memory by removing selected KV entries. Progressive quantization retains all tokens and instead changes their storage precision.

The approaches are complementary but have different correctness and kernel requirements.

### CPU or remote KV-cache offloading

Related to #33526.

Offloading moves older blocks out of GPU memory. It can save more HBM, but retrieving an offloaded block adds data-transfer latency. Progressive quantization keeps all configured precision tiers in GPU memory and targets reduced storage and attention bandwidth.

Offloading could eventually be represented as an additional terminal tier, but it is not required for the initial precision-tier abstraction.

### Application-level context truncation or retrieval

Applications can truncate old messages, summarize conversation history, or use retrieval to reconstruct relevant context. These techniques change the model input and are not a transparent replacement for retaining the full KV cache.

---

## Additional context

Related issues and roadmap items:

- #22195 — layer-wise mixed-precision KV-cache configuration
- #32220 — NVFP4 KV-cache support
- #5751 — sparse KV-cache framework
- #33526 — progressive KV-cache CPU onloading
- #48168 — Q3 2026 roadmap, including production KV-cache compression

This proposal is intentionally narrower than a general sparse-cache or tiered-offloading framework. The key requested abstraction is the ability for blocks belonging to the same attention layer to use different storage formats based on block age.

The proposed `20% BF16 / 20% FP8 / 60% NVFP4` policy is only one illustrative configuration. The implementation should also support policies whose highest tier is already quantized, such as `20% FP8 / 80% NVFP4`.

The policy should therefore be modeled as an ordered list:

```text
[(format, age range), ...]
```

rather than as a special BF16 cache with optional quantized older blocks.

Feedback would be especially useful on whether this should be implemented as:

1. an extension of the existing KV-cache specification and allocator;
2. a specialized cache manager;
3. an attention-backend capability;
4. or part of a more general KV-cache compression policy interface.

title: [Bugfix][Quantization] Dispatch FP8_PER_CHANNEL_PER_TOKEN in ModelOpt MIXED_PRECISION
body:
## Purpose

`ModelOptFp8PcPtLinearMethod` is defined and `FP8_PER_CHANNEL_PER_TOKEN` is a recognised
ModelOpt `quant_algo`, but `ModelOptMixedPrecisionConfig.get_quant_method` has no branch for it.
The algo resolves correctly from `quantized_layers`, matches none of
`FP8` / `NVFP4` / `W4A16_NVFP4` / `MXFP8` / `FP8_PB_WO`, and falls through to
`UnquantizedLinearMethod`.

The layer therefore never registers `weight_scale`, and a checkpoint that carries one fails to
load:

```
ValueError: There is no module or parameter named
'...input_mix_weight_up.weight_scale' in <Model>.
The available parameters belonging to ...input_mix_weight_up (ReplicatedLinear) are:
{'...input_mix_weight_up.weight'}
```

Two lines, mirroring the branches immediately around it.

**Why per-channel matters rather than just using `FP8_PB_WO`:** blockwise FP8 requires both
dimensions divisible by 128. Shapes that fail that constraint have no working FP8 path at all
today. Concretely, on Qwen3.8-Flash-Next the hyper-connection projections are
`(320, 10240)`, `(10240, 320)` and `(4, 10240)` — `out % 128` is 64 or 4, `in % 128` is 64 —
so every one falls off the fast CUTLASS blockwise kernel. Per-output-channel scales carry no
block constraint, and they also slice cleanly across a fused `MergedColumnParallelLinear`,
which a blockwise scale cannot when a shard is narrower than one block.

## Test Plan

1. New unit test `test_modelopt_mixed_precision_dispatches_fp8_pc_pt_method` in
   `tests/quantization/test_modelopt.py`, placed with the existing mixed-precision dispatch
   tests. No GPU, no checkpoint — builds a `ModelOptMixedPrecisionConfig` declaring one layer as
   `FP8_PER_CHANNEL_PER_TOKEN` and asserts `get_quant_method` returns
   `ModelOptFp8PcPtLinearMethod`.

   ```
   pytest tests/quantization/test_modelopt.py -k mixed_precision
   ```

2. End-to-end: serve a `MIXED_PRECISION` checkpoint whose `quantized_layers` marks a set of
   linears `FP8_PER_CHANNEL_PER_TOKEN`, with matching `weight` + `weight_scale` tensors.

## Test Result

**Before** — the server fails during weight loading with the `ValueError` above, on a checkpoint
whose config and tensors are internally consistent.

**After** — the layers dispatch to `ModelOptFp8PcPtLinearMethod`, the checkpoint loads, and the
model serves normally. Verified on a GB10 (sm_121) with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, 96 hyper-connection
projections converted to per-channel FP8 (mean weight reconstruction error 2.21%): coherent
output, and speculative-decode acceptance unchanged at 57.4% against 56.6% for the BF16 baseline.

Dispatch confirmed directly:

```
dispatched to: ModelOptFp8PcPtLinearMethod
```

For transparency on scope: the conversion was performance-neutral for those particular shapes on
that hardware, which is a property of the shapes rather than of this fix. The bug being fixed
here is that the scheme is unreachable at all through `MIXED_PRECISION`.

title: [Test][Quantization] Fix W4A16 NVFP4 auto kernel selection test
body:
## Purpose

Follow-up to #59135. 

> The test seems to indicate that auto is meant to resolve to Marlin? Does this test fail?

It does not fail in CI, but only because the quantization shard runs on H200 (SM90), where `auto` resolves to Marlin. `test_modelopt_w4a16_respects_linear_backend` had an `("auto", MarlinNvFp4LinearKernel)` case and a docstring saying `use_a16=True` "defaults to Marlin". Both predate the selection logic #53014 added, which makes `auto` prefer the FlashInfer CuTe-DSL kernel on SM100/SM103 when FlashInfer's BF16 x FP4 GEMM is available. On a B200 with FlashInfer >= 0.6.18 the same case fails. 

What changed, all in `tests/quantization/test_modelopt.py`:

- `test_modelopt_w4a16_respects_linear_backend`: dropped the `auto` case and the `if linear_backend != "auto"` guard around the `is_supported` skip that only existed for it. The docstring now says an explicit backend wins over the `auto` default, without claiming what `auto` picks.
- New `test_modelopt_w4a16_auto_prefers_cutedsl_on_sm100`: patches `current_platform.get_device_capability` and `has_flashinfer_bf16_fp4` so the `auto` branch of `init_nvfp4_linear_kernel(use_a16=True)` is asserted on any CUDA GPU, independent of the CI hardware. Four cases: SM90 gives Marlin, SM100 and SM103 with FlashInfer give CuTe-DSL, SM100 without FlashInfer gives Marlin.

Test only, no functional changes.

I checked the open PRs touching NVFP4 W4A16 selection or this test file (#44671, #44672, #47674, #54614, #55405, #56553, #59460); none change the `auto` case or `test_modelopt_w4a16_respects_linear_backend`.

I used Claude Code to trace the selection path and draft the test, and reviewed every changed line myself.

## Test Plan

```bash
pre-commit run --files tests/quantization/test_modelopt.py
python -m pytest tests/quantization/test_modelopt.py -k "w4a16" -v
```

Run on an NVIDIA B200 (SM100, driver 580.95.05) with torch 2.13.0+cu130, FlashInfer 0.7.0.post1 and nvidia-cutlass-dsl 4.7.1, so `has_flashinfer_bf16_fp4()` is True. vLLM is the nightly wheel for cb6458c5ce, whose Python code is identical to this branch's base (the one commit between them is CI-only), with this branch's `tests/` mounted on top.

To confirm the motivation, the pre-fix version of the test file (from ab5266769e) was run with `-k "respects_linear_backend and auto"`, then this branch's file with `-k "w4a16"`.

No model evaluation needed; the change is to a test.

## Test Result

All pre-commit hooks pass.

Before the fix, on the B200, the `auto` case fails because the selector returns CuTe-DSL:

```
tests/quantization/test_modelopt.py::test_modelopt_w4a16_respects_linear_backend[auto-MarlinNvFp4LinearKernel] FAILED
>       assert isinstance(kernel, kernel_cls)
E       AssertionError: assert False
E        +  where False = isinstance(<vllm.model_executor.kernels.linear.nvfp4.flashinfer.FlashInferCuteDslNvFp4W4A16LinearKernel object at 0x2af915ed5160>, <class 'vllm.model_executor.kernels.linear.nvfp4.marlin.MarlinNvFp4LinearKernel'>)
================ 1 failed, 39 deselected, 15 warnings in 4.24s =================
```

After the fix, on the same machine, all 12 W4A16-related tests pass, nothing skipped:

```
collected 43 items / 31 deselected / 12 selected
tests/quantization/test_modelopt.py::test_modelopt_mixed_precision_dispatches_every_linear_algo[W4A16_NVFP4] PASSED
tests/quantization/test_modelopt.py::test_modelopt_nvfp4_config_dispatches_w4a16_method PASSED
tests/quantization/test_modelopt.py::test_modelopt_w4a16_respects_linear_backend[humming-HummingNvFp4LinearKernel] PASSED
tests/quantization/test_modelopt.py::test_modelopt_w4a16_respects_linear_backend[flashinfer_cutedsl-FlashInferCuteDslNvFp4W4A16LinearKernel] PASSED
tests/quantization/test_modelopt.py::test_modelopt_w4a16_auto_prefers_cutedsl_on_sm100[90-True-MarlinNvFp4LinearKernel] PASSED
tests/quantization/test_modelopt.py::test_modelopt_w4a16_auto_prefers_cutedsl_on_sm100[100-True-FlashInferCuteDslNvFp4W4A16LinearKernel] PASSED
tests/quantization/test_modelopt.py::test_modelopt_w4a16_auto_prefers_cutedsl_on_sm100[103-True-FlashInferCuteDslNvFp4W4A16LinearKernel] PASSED
tests/quantization/test_modelopt.py::test_modelopt_w4a16_auto_prefers_cutedsl_on_sm100[100-False-MarlinNvFp4LinearKernel] PASSED
tests/quantization/test_modelopt.py::test_modelopt_nvfp4_moe_dispatches_to_marlin_when_w4a16[NVFP4-False-False] PASSED
tests/quantization/test_modelopt.py::test_modelopt_nvfp4_moe_dispatches_to_marlin_when_w4a16[W4A16_NVFP4-True-True] PASSED
tests/quantization/test_modelopt.py::test_modelopt_mixed_precision_dispatches_linear_layer[W4A16_NVFP4-expected_weight1-None] PASSED
tests/quantization/test_modelopt.py::test_modelopt_mixed_precision_builds_w4a16_sibling_config PASSED
================ 12 passed, 31 deselected, 15 warnings in 5.94s ================
```

title: [Roadmap] vLLM Roadmap Q4 2026
body:
In [#32455](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/32455), we broke down vLLM's goals into various special interest groups (SIGs). Building on the [Q3 roadmap](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/48168), please find below each SIG's Q4 roadmap. You can find regular meetings of these SIGs on the public vLLM calendar.

## Key takeaway

* **Agentic Workload:** Q3 established Model Runner V2 as the default and brought production-ready Rust frontend and distributed KV offloading support. Q4 focuses on making optimized agentic serving easier to deploy: better day-0 performance, tuned production recipes, adaptive speculative decoding, richer agent hints, and fault tolerance across hardware.
* **Ecosystem:** We are expanding low-precision serving and checkpoint conversion across NVIDIA and AMD, strengthening speculative decoding and RL integration, and advancing Agentic API and vLLM-Omni. Frontier models and new hardware need a clear path from initial support to validated, optimized production configurations.
* **OSS Maintenance:** We are simplifying engine and model interfaces, completing quantization dispatch refactors, and improving CI coverage, time to signal, security, and performance evaluation. Agent-assisted review and better test-quality checks should help the community maintain a growing model, feature, and hardware matrix.

### SIG Core ([Meeting Notes](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1x36yhn655LiuV6bPK2C1M-6jfMzgXDLQf2PIngJndgc/edit?tab=t.0))

- [ ] Fully remove Model Runner V1 and close the remaining [Model Runner V2 gaps](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/47172).
- [ ] Implement [extensible KV cache support](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/56492), pluggable `KVCacheConfigBuilder` implementations for models, and better cache-grouping heuristics for sliding-window attention speculators.
- [ ] Refactor CUDA graphs: separate prefill/decode graph sizes; clarify capture, dispatch, and padding semantics, including adaptive verification and sequence parallelism; and simplify encoder and DeepSeek V4.1 prefill-skipping graphs. Validate prefill graph sizing against padding overhead and performance regressions.
- [ ] Simplify and harden the engine's model loop, data-parallel flow, and scheduler, and improve streaming-input reliability.
- [ ] Reduce coupling between model implementations and the engine through a clearer model interface.
- [ ] Advance the Rust frontend toward default use, including resolving Responses API readiness and parity requirements.
- [ ] Add native per-step observability through [forward-pass metrics](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/52061), in collaboration with Dynamo.

* Aspirational work:
  - Simplify KV connector interfaces through standardized KV layouts, including exploring parallel interfaces.
  - Revisit automatic prefix caching and investigate lookahead EAGLE block caching as a replacement for block dropping.
  - Explore a more comprehensive scheduler redesign beyond the immediate cleanup.

### SIG Large Scale Serving ([Meeting Notes](https://docs.google.com/document/d/15A9zid75c41pcn8hzIKXOW2R6VFgeUfGuIMq-ebgEEI/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.prqroxfe0fr1))

- [ ] Extend agent hints across routers and KV connectors with Dynamo and llm-d: multi-tenancy, cache-tier TTLs, filesystem eviction, and request-level control of prefetching, eviction, and selective offloading.
- [ ] Publish production recipes with clear explanations of deployment and performance tradeoffs, including disaggregated prefill/decode and KV offloading.
- [ ] Harden numerical fault handling, including NaNs, and expert-parallel recovery through restart and scale-down; integrate recovery with llm-d and Dynamo.
- [ ] Achieve state-of-the-art agentic workload performance for priority models across AMD and new hardware, including Rubin and MI455X.
- [ ] Integrate native [forward-pass metrics](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/52061) into the serving observability work with Dynamo.

* Proposed work: define the scope and milestones for AFD.

### SIG Model Performance ([Meeting Notes](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1A1TOuCTPQ_72npOSzhWKfYOmDIF7OoagLGaL8gHe1TQ/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.wmm9txlfqo9w))

- [ ] Improve day-0 performance and the workflow from initial model support to optimized agentic serving configurations.
- [ ] Continue sprints for frontier models, including DeepSeek V4.1, GLM 5.3, and Qwen3.8, with continuous model and feature tracking.
- [ ] Optimize Vera Rubin performance and publish reproducible serving recipes.
- [ ] Expand FP4 KV cache support to more models and add disk-backed KV offloading.
- [ ] Continue the [performance-evaluation dashboard](https://vllm-ci-dashboard.vercel.app/perf) and broaden regression tracking with SIG CI.

* Proposals to evaluate: bring `vllm-recipes` into the main repository, restructure model-specific tests, and clarify the scope and feasibility of deprecating vLLM IR and custom Torch compile passes.

### SIG Spec Decode ([Meeting Notes](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1DlgW4dWZyGup_BOZm24Bo50AFIiQgPXfSLqMGDLt6Ic/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.1efi34fxtsr2))

- [ ] Improve HMA and heterogeneous attention support between drafter and verifier. Make sliding-window drafters compose efficiently with different target attention types and reduce KV cache padding and memory overhead.
- [ ] Polish adaptive verification and extend support to Mamba2, GDN, and QSA. Research oracle verification to quantify remaining performance opportunities and guide optimization.
- [ ] Migrate speculative model code to Flat Model, then optimize fusion and kernels for low-latency inference, including rejection sampling.
- [ ] Enable block rejection sampling and probabilistic verification by default.
- [ ] Finalize `open-spec-config` configuration details for popular draft algorithms and implement draft-model loading.
- [ ] Improve configuration ergonomics and robustness with tool calling, reasoning, and structured outputs. Enabling speculative decoding itself by default remains an aspiration.

### SIG CI ([Meeting Notes](https://docs.google.com/document/u/2/d/18VJOuEyAZmRVILWpOtYx5jC4iFZLwjHVw5TAdfJnjXQ/edit?tab=t.0))

- [ ] Collect test-coverage data and maintain a feature-combination matrix, including prefill/decode disaggregation.
- [ ] Bring time to signal toward 30 minutes through automatic test selection, pytest-level granularity, automatic sharding, and default job timeouts.
- [ ] Migrate remaining four-L4 jobs to H200 MIG, reduce Docker build/pull and environment-setup overhead, and retire obsolete jobs for old models.
- [ ] Improve infrastructure-failure detection, quarantine, and retries, and carry forward flaky-test management.
- [ ] Perform offensive security testing of vLLM and make CI safe for projects throughout the vLLM ecosystem.
- [ ] Expand performance and accuracy evaluation to disaggregated serving and TPU, including InferenceX-style benchmark sweeps and throughput/latency Pareto curves.
- [ ] Develop agent-assisted reviewers and CI shepherds, with checks for unit-test quality.
- [ ] Clarify and document CI trigger paths and coverage for RDNA, XPU, and other accelerators, including projects maintained outside the main repository, to reduce cross-backend breakage.

### SIG Quantization

- [ ] **LUT-B (W3A8) on Rubin:** finalize the NVIDIA format specification, including tile sizes, codebooks, and scales ([Model Optimizer #2204](https://github.com/NVIDIA/Model-Optimizer/issues/2204), [compressed-tensors #801](https://github.com/vllm-project/compressed-tensors/pull/801)); provide an [LLM Compressor calibration recipe](https://github.com/vllm-project/llm-compressor/pull/3018), validated checkpoints, and optimized dense/MoE kernels with MXFP8 activations.
- [ ] **Production FP4 and lower-bit KV caches:** publish accuracy evaluations and recommended configurations for priority models. Cover long-context interactive serving and high-concurrency data generation, and compose with hybrid attention, speculative drafters, NIXL disaggregation, and tiered offloading.
  - Expand NVFP4 coverage across FlashMLA/DSA sparse attention, FA4, Rubin kernels, and [SM8x–SM12x enablement](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/46963).
  - Advance ROCm low-bit KV work, including [UltraQuant](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/57057) and the [Octave KV proposal](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/59773), with platform-specific validation rather than assuming one format fits every backend.
- [ ] **Checkpoint requantization:** complete the [online quantization from arbitrary precision roadmap](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/59062) through a common online quantization API, including [requantization](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/55684), [activation QuantKey overrides](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/51808), [shared experts](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/55686), and [MLA `kv_b_proj`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/55741). Initial conversions include MXFP8 to FP8 per-channel/block on Hopper and MI300, and FP8/NVFP4 to MXFP4 across vendors.
- [ ] **Unified dispatch and inspectability:** finish QuantKey/QuantConfig adoption in [Quark](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/56099), [ModelOpt MoE](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/55339), and compressed-tensors. Declare weight and activation QuantKeys across methods, complete the [MoE oracle and linear-kernel migration](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/54959), extend QuantKey into `FusedMoEQuantDesc`, and log selected kernels/backends by layer type.
- [ ] **Kernel consolidation:** make [Humming the default over Marlin on Hopper](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/56997), then extend to SM10x/SM12x. Consolidate autotuning configurations and benchmark overlapping CuTe-DSL, b12x, FlashInfer TRTLLM, Marlin, Qutlass, and Humming paths to choose per-architecture defaults and retire superseded paths.
- [ ] **Compression ecosystem:** deliver day-0 NVFP4/MXFP4 checkpoints for priority models, advance [MoNe](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/50415) and [REAP expert pruning](https://github.com/vllm-project/llm-compressor/pull/2906), and make `convert_checkpoint` the general format-conversion entry point.
- [ ] **Quality validation:** add quantized-model accuracy CI, tensor-parallel parity checks for online quantization, and quantized weight-reload correctness checks with the RL ecosystem.

* Research directions: LUT-B attention support, FP4 with rotations through QuTLASS, HIGGS, and QAD. Continue evaluating [legacy format deprecation](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/30136).

### SIG AMD

- [ ] Close frontier-model prefill, decode, speculative decoding, and long-context performance gaps on ROCm, prioritizing DeepSeek V4/V4.1, Kimi K3, GLM 5.x, and Qwen3.x.
- [ ] Productionize context parallelism for sparse, MLA, and hybrid-attention models, and harden prefill/decode disaggregation and KV transfer.
- [ ] Improve multi-tier KV offloading across GPU, host memory, SSD, and distributed storage, including Mooncake, MoRI/UMBP, and NIXL integrations.
- [ ] Expand AITER kernels and fused FP8/MXFP8/FP4/MXFP4 execution paths, with automatic backend selection and fewer AMD-specific configuration requirements.
- [ ] Strengthen AMD/Quark day-0 support: FP4 and FP8-PTPC for priority CDNA models, plus INT4 and other low-bit formats for priority RDNA models. Coordinate online requantization and flexible activation QuantKey overrides with SIG Quantization.
- [ ] Advance UltraQuant and MXFP4 KV-cache/attention support on ROCm, and support MTP, EAGLE, and DFlash for priority models, including quantized draft heads.
- [ ] Maintain MI355X as the primary performance platform while closing MI300X/MI325X gaps, expanding RDNA support where applicable, and improving AMD CI parity, performance regression coverage, and ROCm release readiness. Document the RDNA validation and CI trigger path with SIG CI.

### SIG Agentic API

- [ ] Deliver [multi-agent APIs](https://github.com/vllm-project/agentic-api/issues/298).
- [ ] Add a [code interpreter tool](https://github.com/vllm-project/agentic-api/issues/308).
- [ ] Use the [shared Rust frontend library](https://github.com/vllm-project/agentic-api/issues/359) for direct vLLM engine inference.
- [ ] Add a [file search tool](https://github.com/vllm-project/agentic-api/pull/278).

### vLLM-Omni

- [ ] Continue optimizing frontier diffusion models, including MiniMax H3.
- [ ] Integrate with RL frameworks, including verl with ve-omni as the training framework.
- [ ] Expand acceleration backends and framework integrations, including FastVideo.
- [ ] Complete the [full-duplex redesign](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-omni/issues/7181), carrying forward Q3 prototyping work.

### RL Ecosystem

- [ ] Execute the [Q4 vLLM × RL roadmap](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/58990): weight updates, training–inference consistency, and feature enablement such as LoRA for RL.
- [ ] Improve day-0 RL support for new models.
- [ ] Refactor weight updates and advance the auxiliary connector design to address correctness at the architectural level, including quantized weight reloads with SIG Quantization.

------

Please leave feedback and comments, and work directly with the relevant SIG areas for deeper collaboration.

title: [RFC]: Layer-Wise Mixed-Precision KV Cache
body:
Status: Draft for discussion. Scope: a four-part vLLM implementation stack (logical dtype, packed allocation, ModelOpt integration, and CPU offloading) plus a separate proposed manager-block optimization. Cache calculations below evaluate the full design including that optimization; none of the four PRs enables it.

## Summary

Allow a model to use different KV-cache formats in different attention layers, initially full FP8 K/V and full NVFP4 K/V. Preserve each layer's logical encoding through dispatch and allocation, and support both attention-only models and hybrid attention/Mamba models using existing attention kernels and the heterogeneous cache-packing infrastructure already used by DeepSeek V4.

This is **layer-wise** mixed precision. FP8 K with NVFP4 V inside the same layer is a separate feature and is not enabled by this RFC.

## Motivation

Layers can have different sensitivity to KV quantization. A checkpoint should be able to retain FP8 in selected layers and use NVFP4 elsewhere, without requiring a model-wide format or changes to attention kernels.

Two runtime assumptions make this difficult:

- Physical tensor dtype alone does not fully describe the KV encoding or scales.
- Legacy hybrid allocation couples attention block sizing to recurrent-state page sizes. Adding attention formats with different byte sizes can increase alignment requirements, padding, and prefix-cache block granularity.

The proposal separates logical encoding from physical page allocation. It enables quality/memory trade-off experiments; it does not prescribe the optimal layer recipe or claim an accuracy improvement for every model.

## Proposed Change

```text
ModelOpt checkpoint recipe       Explicit global KV dtype override
             |                                  |
             +----------> Effective per-layer dtype
                                      |
                          AttentionSpec.cache_dtype
                              /                 \
                 Backend dtype dispatch     Exact cache-page specs
                          |                         |
                 Existing FP8/NVFP4 kernels  Packed block-pool allocation
```

### 1. Preserve Logical Dtype

Add `AttentionSpec.cache_dtype` and the generic `QuantizationConfig.get_kv_cache_dtype(prefix)` hook, defaulting to `None`. Preserve logical dtype and quantization mode during spec merges, and reject conflicting formats.

FlashInfer uses an explicit global KV dtype first, then a concrete per-spec dtype. An ambiguous quantized spec fails clearly instead of guessing its encoding. Existing unquantized behavior and skip-layer precedence are retained.

### 2. Reuse DeepSeek V4 Cache Packing

DeepSeek V4 already needs caches with different page sizes, such as MLA, indexer, and sliding-window caches. vLLM's existing infrastructure represents those pages separately and packs compatible layers into cache groups. We reuse that mechanism for pages whose sizes differ because of FP8/NVFP4 encoding.

| Existing mechanism | Reuse for layer-wise mixed precision |
|---|---|
| `UniformTypeKVCacheSpecs` | Retain each layer's exact spec and page size within a compatible group. |
| `_get_packed_kv_cache_groups()` | Group layers by compatible cache behavior, without requiring identical page sizes. |
| Block-outer allocation and per-layer offsets/strides | Place FP8 and NVFP4 pages side by side and expose each layer's view to its existing kernel. |
| Shared block pool | Size rows for the widest packed group; a block ID belongs to one group at a time. |

Here, "uniform type" means compatible token-slot requirements, not necessarily the same encoding or byte size. Attention and Mamba state still retain their distinct cache semantics; we do not merge them into one attention spec.

The packed-group builder and core allocator are reused without changes in this stack. The additions preserve per-layer dtype, enable a compatible layout, avoid premature page-size unification, and consume checkpoint recipes. This does **not** reuse DeepSeek's model-specific compression algorithm, attention kernels, or token-selection policy.

Add a default-disabled `has_layerwise_kv_cache()` capability. When supported, reuse `UniformTypeKVCacheSpecs` and block-outer allocation to pack exact per-layer attention and state-cache pages. Bypass legacy hybrid page-size unification only for compatible configurations; incompatible layouts retain the existing aligned-page fallback.

The shared pool row must fit the widest packed group. Exact per-layer sizes therefore remove per-layer padding, but **do not eliminate pool-row slack**. Wrapped Mamba specs must still initialize the Mamba SSU backend.

The current implementation keeps the manager block equal to the supported kernel page: P64 in the validated FlashInfer NVFP4 configuration. The full design additionally considers larger manager blocks containing multiple P64 kernel pages, as described below. These larger blocks require a separately validated subpage layout; they are not currently supported merely by setting a larger `--block-size`.

### 3. Enable ModelOpt Recipes

Consume schema-v1 `kv_cache_quantized_layers` metadata, resolve attention-layer prefixes, and map FP8 to `fp8_e4m3` and NVFP4 to `nvfp4`. Validate invalid or incomplete recipes and preserve legacy metadata handling.

With `--kv-cache-dtype auto`, use the checkpoint recipe. An explicit global dtype overrides it. Weight quantization remains independent of the KV recipe. Producer-side support is tracked in [Model-Optimizer #2272](https://github.com/NVIDIA/Model-Optimizer/pull/2272).

### 4. Preserve Packed Layouts for CPU Offloading

The built-in `OffloadingConnector` normally requests `LBHNC`, which can bypass packed hybrid allocation and select padded pages that cannot be split into supported kernel pages. For configurations advertising `has_layerwise_kv_cache()`, let the allocator select the compatible layout instead. Ordinary non-layerwise configurations keep their existing layout requirement; HiSparse retains its explicit requirement.

Reuse the existing packed-row CPU transfer path to preserve quantized attention payloads, scales, and recurrent-state bytes without format conversion. This supports store/reload with the same model, recipe, and parallel topology. It still transfers the complete backing row, including unused space; it does not implement compact CPU slots, new transfer kernels, or manager-block optimization.

### 5. Proposed Manager-Block Optimization (Separate Follow-Up)

Exact per-layer sizes alone do not resolve shared-pool slack. Size the manager block so several small attention pages fit the allocation size needed by a state group, while keeping attention kernel pages at P64. Attention and state groups still own separate pool blocks; this does not co-locate a live state and attention payload in the same row.

The design estimate evaluates manager-block multiples of 64 through 1,024 tokens, scores the complete request footprint at the configured maximum sequence length, and selects the smallest candidate within 1% of the minimum. Production candidates must first pass backend, subpage-layout, and cross-group validation. For the Nano example below, the estimate selects 448 tokens: seven P64 attention pages require 525 KiB, closely matching a 521-KiB Mamba state.

This is the intended optimization on top of the core stack, not a claim that the current PRs implement it. Before enabling it, validate multiple physical pages, kernel-block IDs, per-layer scale/stride indexing, prefix-cache boundaries, CUDA graphs, and end-to-end generation. The manager/prefix boundary is 448 tokens in this example, not 64; kernel page size alone does not establish cache-hit granularity.

## Compatibility and Limits

- No new kernels, extension ABI changes, or asynchronous compression manager.
- Infrastructure hooks default to disabled; only ModelOpt integration activates this feature in the proposed stack.
- Existing backend hardware, format, head-size, and layout restrictions apply.
- The CPU-offload follow-up covers the built-in connector on a fixed model, recipe, and topology. NIXL prefill/decode transfer, LMCache, secondary tiers, and cross-topology canonical offloading remain unvalidated.
- MLA spec metadata is preserved, but mixed-format MLA serving is not validated or claimed as supported by these experiments.
- The implemented intermediate path uses a P64 manager block; the stacked design can use a larger manager block while retaining P64 kernel pages. Actual prefix reuse also depends on cache-group and recurrent-state constraints. No measured cache-hit-rate gain is claimed.
- The recorded P64-only Nano configuration remains state-row dominated. The stacked calculation addresses that slack, but its projected memory reduction is not a measured serving-capacity result.

## Memory Accounting: Same Mixed Recipe

For Nano TP4 with three FP8 K/V layers, three NVFP4 K/V layers, and 23 Mamba layers, compare **legacy aligned allocation** against **the full stacked design: exact-page packing plus manager-block optimization**, keeping logical dtypes fixed. These are CPU allocator-source/design estimates, not GPU peak-memory measurements. The control retains recipe support but disables the layout preference and hybrid-alignment bypass; unmodified upstream cannot consume the recipe.

MiB per rank per request; waste = allocation minus useful payload:

| Tokens | Useful Payload, Both | Legacy Allocation | Legacy Waste | Stacked Allocation | Stacked Waste |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 4,096 | 28.09 | 35.06 | 6.97 | 28.71 | 0.62 |
| 16,384 | 42.15 | 63.75 | 21.60 | 42.55 | 0.40 |
| 131,072 | 173.40 | 315.56 | 142.16 | 173.80 | 0.40 |

Accounting includes quantized attention payload/scales and two resident Mamba states per layer, following `align`-mode request budgeting. Waste includes per-layer page padding, last-block token rounding, and unused shared-pool row space. It excludes weights, graphs, activations, metadata, prefix sharing, inactive cached requests, and transient extra states. The 128K row is a sizing projection, not a validated serving run.

Legacy unification produces 2,176-token FP8 blocks and 1,088-token NVFP4 blocks. The stacked estimate selects a 448-token manager block for all three lengths, while kernel pages remain P64. The attention group fills a 525-KiB row; state-owned rows leave only 4 KiB of slack each. Estimated allocation is `525 KiB * (ceil(tokens / 448) + 46)`, with the 46 state rows accounting for two states across 23 layers.

For transparency, the **current P64-only intermediate implementation** still estimates 55.97 / 153.65 / 1,065.40 MiB allocation and 27.88 / 111.50 / 892.00 MiB waste at these lengths. Its attention-owned rows reserve 521 KiB for 75 KiB of payload. Those are not the full stacked-design results and must not be presented as memory savings.

The replay uses grouping/spec source at `513d810e82` and the historical optimizer's candidate/tie-break policy at `287e63a837`. Ten accounting tests pass, including candidate selection and byte conservation. P64 groups/page sizes match the recorded GPU snapshot; the 448-token layout is a design projection, not validated tensor views or an end-to-end runtime. Both legacy-control serving validation and stacked-layout validation remain outstanding.

## Expected Benefits

- **Quality flexibility:** retain higher precision in sensitive layers while compressing less sensitive layers. Actual quality depends on the recipe and requires model-specific evaluation; no accuracy scores are disclosed here.
- **Smaller attention payloads:** avoid forcing every layer to use the higher-precision format. Overall capacity gains depend on allocator layout and state-cache requirements.
- **Infrastructure reuse:** extend an existing heterogeneous-cache mechanism rather than introduce a ModelOpt-specific allocator or new attention kernels.
- **Serving compatibility:** retain existing compile, CUDA graph, and backend execution paths, with explicit dtype overrides and layout fallback behavior.

## Validation

Unit/regression coverage includes dtype merges and precedence, recipe parsing, exact page offsets and strides, multiple physical pages, fallback layouts, and wrapped-Mamba dispatch. The September 16 rebased stack passed 185 tests on GB300. A subsequent typing-only fix passed local mypy checks for all three PRs and full upstream pre-commit for PR 1; those GPU suites were not rerun for that fix.

Earlier TP4 serving smokes passed on Qwen3.8-27B (7 FP8 + 9 NVFP4 attention layers) and Nano v3 (3 FP8 + 3 NVFP4), with CUDA graph capture and 512-token generation with finite logprobs. These are pre-rebase functional smokes, not benchmark-accuracy results or a fresh validation of the current heads.

Earlier Nano serving measurements showed broadly comparable throughput to homogeneous FP8 and NVFP4 under the tested workloads, with a latency regression in one long-context, low-concurrency case. All formats used the same packed allocator: this does not establish zero overhead or compare the allocator against unmodified upstream allocation. Detailed experimental figures are intentionally omitted from this RFC.

The CPU-offload follow-up passed 541 focused regression tests (one ROCm-only skip), plus Nano TP4 cache round trips with FULL and PIECEWISE graphs and 512-token generation. Cold, CPU-reloaded, and fully recomputed outputs matched exactly within each successful process. Default unpatched offloading reproduced the padded-page startup failure; explicit `BLHNC` and the patched default both enabled reloads. Strict cross-process comparison matrices still failed because cold outputs varied across some independent launches, including unpatched no-offload controls. Reload transparency is validated for the tested configuration; full cross-launch reproducibility is not. These are functional checks, not benchmark-accuracy claims.

Before final integration, rerun serving smokes on the final rebased stack, retain explicit coverage of homogeneous formats and unsupported-layout fallback, and investigate the observed cross-launch cold-output variability separately from CPU reload correctness.

## Rollout and Discussion

The implementation is organized as four dependent PRs:

1. [#56155: Logical per-layer dtype](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/56155).
2. [#56156: Packed heterogeneous allocation](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/56156).
3. [#56116: ModelOpt integration](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/56116).
4. [#59265: CPU offloading for packed layer-wise KV cache](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/59265) (draft; depends on #56116).

Manager-block optimization and validated P64 subpage addressing remain a separate proposed follow-up, outside these four PRs. No PR is linked for that optimization; it is included only in this RFC's design-level memory estimates. The CPU-offload PR does not change those estimates or reduce backing-row slack.

The main review questions are whether the generic hooks and fallback policy are appropriate, how to validate larger manager blocks without changing kernel pages, and what additional backend coverage is needed before expansion. The full stack must pass memory, prefix-reuse, CUDA graph, and serving validation before its projected savings are claimed as runtime results.

title: [Performance]: FlashInfer NVFP4 KV cache causal prefill is ~1.7-1.8x slower than FP8 on SM120
body:
### Summary

On NVIDIA consumer Blackwell (SM120), FlashInfer attention with an NVFP4 KV cache shows a significant causal prefill regression compared with an FP8 KV cache.

In a matched profiler segment with the same 48 causal paged-prefill kernel calls, the NVFP4 path took about **145.8 ms**, while the FP8 path took about **84.0 ms**. This makes NVFP4 prefill approximately **1.74x slower** (about 1.7-1.8x across measurements).

The profiler indicates that the current SM120 path uses BF16 Q with packed NVFP4 KV:

```text
NVFP4:
BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheKernel<
  ...,
  __nv_bfloat16,      # Q
  __nv_fp4x2_e2m1,    # KV
  __nv_bfloat16,      # output
  ...
>

FP8:
BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheKernel<
  ...,
  __nv_bfloat16,      # Q
  __nv_fp8_e4m3,      # KV
  __nv_bfloat16,      # output
  ...
>
```

The regression appears to come from the existing SM120 NVFP4 software unpack/dequant path: packed FP4 KV values and their FP8 block scales must be unpacked, converted, and scaled before the BF16 QK/PV computation. Prefill is compute-heavy, so the KV bandwidth reduction does not compensate for this per-element conversion overhead.

### Environment

```text
GPU: NVIDIA RTX PRO 5000 Blackwell, compute capability 12.0 (SM120)
PyTorch: 2.10.0+cu129
CUDA: 12.9
FlashInfer: 0.6.15
Attention backend: FLASHINFER
KV cache layout: HND
Model dtype / Q dtype on this path: BF16
KV cache modes compared: nvfp4 and fp8_e4m3
```

The vLLM code includes the recently added NVFP4 KV cache path. The NVFP4 cache is represented as packed E2M1 data plus one FP8 block-scale value per 16 head-dimension elements.

### Kernel-level profile

A comparable trace segment was selected from each profile. Both segments contain exactly 48 causal prefill calls:

| Metric | NVFP4 KV | FP8 KV | NVFP4 / FP8 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Causal paged-prefill calls | 48 | 48 | 1.00x |
| Causal paged-prefill total | 145.81 ms | 84.03 ms | 1.74x |
| Mean per call | 3.04 ms | 1.75 ms | 1.74x |
| CUTLASS GEMM total in the same segment | 93.61 ms | 96.69 ms | 0.97x |
| All GPU kernels in the segment | 297.73 ms | 238.45 ms | 1.25x |

The similar CUTLASS GEMM time suggests that the model's weight/MoE kernels are not the primary source of this difference. Most of the additional GPU time is inside `BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheKernel`.

### Decode and KV append observations

The same profiles show that NVFP4 is beneficial for decode:

| Kernel | NVFP4 KV | FP8 KV |
|---|---:|---:|
| Single-token/decode paged attention | ~9.63 us/call | ~12.35 us/call |
| KV append/write | ~8.39 us/call | ~3.01 us/call |

NVFP4 decode is about 22% faster in this workload because decode is more bandwidth-bound. The NVFP4 append kernel is about 2.8x slower because it performs quantization, packing, block-scale generation, and slot mapping, but its cumulative cost is only around 7 ms and is not the end-to-end bottleneck.

### End-to-end capacity stress result

With 30 concurrent requests:

| KV dtype | Completed | Preemptions | Peak running | Peak cache | Wall time |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| NVFP4 | 30/30 | 0 | 30 | 68.6% | 102.3 s |
| FP8 | 30/30 | 6 | 24 | 97.6% | 65.4 s |

NVFP4 provides the expected capacity benefit and avoids preemption, but the causal-prefill regression dominates this particular workload.

### Expected behavior / proposal

On SM120, the packed NVFP4 KV representation matches the hardware block-scaled FP4 MMA layout well. An optimized path could:

1. quantize Q to per-16-block NVFP4 on the fly;
2. execute QK directly with SM120 block-scaled NVFP4 MMA;
3. avoid expanding K through the FP4 -> FP16/BF16 conversion chain before QK;
4. retain the existing dequantized P x V path where the V-scale axis does not match the MMA reduction axis.

This is similar to the A4Q approach demonstrated for SM120/SM121, where an opt-in FlashInfer kernel uses FP4 Q x FP4 K block-scaled MMA.

Would the vLLM maintainers be interested in tracking or integrating an optimized FlashInfer A4Q-style path for NVFP4 KV prefill on SM120? At minimum, it would be useful to document that the current NVFP4 KV path trades substantial prefill performance for capacity/decode benefits on this architecture.

### Additional notes

- The NVFP4 cache itself is correctly compact: packed FP4 data plus FP8 scales uses about 56.25% of FP8 KV storage, giving an expected capacity ratio of about 1.78x.
- The two profiler JSON files contain more than one non-contiguous capture interval, so the comparison above uses matched segments instead of comparing total trace file size or total event counts.
- Full profiler JSON files can be provided if useful.
- Related NVFP4 KV integration discussion: #49011 and #32220.

Speculative Decoding: Exploiting Speculative Execution for Accelerating Seq2seq Generation
body: We propose Speculative Decoding (SpecDec), for the first time ever, to formally study exploiting the idea of speculative execution to accelerate autoregressive (AR) decoding. Speculative Decoding has two innovations: Spec-Drafter -- an independent model specially optimized for efficient and accurate drafting -- and Spec-Verification -- a reliable method for verifying the drafted tokens efficiently in the decoding paradigm. Experimental results on various seq2seq tasks including machine translation and abstractive summarization show our approach can achieve around $5\times$ speedup for the popular Transformer architectures with comparable generation quality to beam search decoding, refreshing the impression that the draft-then-verify paradigm introduces only $1.4\times$$\sim$$2\times$ speedup. In addition to the remarkable speedup, we also demonstrate 3 additional advantages of SpecDec, revealing its practical value for accelerating generative models in real-world applications. Our models and codes are available at https://github.com/hemingkx/SpecDec.

title: Component-Aware Self-Speculative Decoding in Hybrid Language Models
body: Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive inference by drafting candidate tokens with a fast model and verifying them in parallel with the target. Self-speculative methods avoid the need for an external drafter but have been studied exclusively in homogeneous Transformer architectures. We introduce component-aware self-speculative decoding, the first method to exploit the internal architectural heterogeneity of hybrid language models, isolating the SSM/linear-attention subgraph as a zero-cost internal draft. We evaluate this on two architecturally distinct hybrid families: Falcon-H1 (parallel: Mamba-2 + attention per layer) and Qwen3.5 (sequential: interleaved linear and attention layers), with a pure Transformer control (Qwen2.5). Parallel hybrids achieve acceptance rates of alpha = 0.68 at draft length k=2 under greedy decoding, while sequential hybrids yield only alpha = 0.038 -- an 18x gap attributable to how each architecture integrates its components. The property is scale-invariant: Falcon-H1 at 3B reproduces the rates observed at 0.5B. We further show that perplexity degradation from a companion ablation study predicts speculative viability without running speculative decoding: a 3.15x ratio (Falcon) maps to alpha = 0.37 at k=4, while 81.96x (Qwen) maps to alpha = 0.019. For sequential hybrids, generic LayerSkip achieves 12x higher acceptance rates than the component-aware strategy. The composition pattern of hybrid models -- not merely the presence of alternative components -- determines whether component-level self-speculation is viable.

title: Speculative Safety-Aware Decoding
body: Despite extensive efforts to align Large Language Models (LLMs) with human values and safety rules, jailbreak attacks that exploit certain vulnerabilities continuously emerge, highlighting the need to strengthen existing LLMs with additional safety properties to defend against these attacks. However, tuning large models has become increasingly resource intensive and may have difficulty ensuring consistent performance. We introduce Speculative Safety-Aware Decoding (SSD), a lightweight decoding-time approach that equips LLMs with the desired safety property while accelerating inference. We assume that there exists a small language model that possesses this desired property. SSD integrates speculative sampling during decoding and leverages the match ratio between the small and composite models to quantify jailbreak risks. This enables SSD to dynamically switch between decoding schemes to prioritize utility or safety, to handle the challenge of different model capacities. The output token is then sampled from a new distribution that combines the distributions of the original and the small models. Experimental results show that SSD successfully equips the large model with the desired safety property, and also allows the model to remain helpful to benign queries. Furthermore, SSD accelerates the inference time, thanks to the speculative sampling design.

title: Tutorial Proposal: Speculative Decoding for Efficient LLM Inference
body: This tutorial presents a comprehensive introduction to Speculative Decoding (SD), an advanced technique for LLM inference acceleration that has garnered significant research interest in recent years. SD is introduced as an innovative decoding paradigm to mitigate the high inference latency stemming from autoregressive decoding in LLMs. At each decoding step, SD efficiently drafts several future tokens and then verifies them in parallel. This approach, unlike traditional autoregressive decoding, facilitates the simultaneous decoding of multiple tokens per step, thereby achieving promising 2x-4x speedups in LLM inference while maintaining original distributions. This tutorial delves into the latest techniques in SD, including draft model architectures and verification strategies. Additionally, it explores the acceleration potential and future research directions in this promising field. We aim for this tutorial to elucidate the current research landscape and offer insights for researchers interested in Speculative Decoding, ultimately contributing to more efficient LLM inference.

title: Speculative Decoding Meets Quantization: Compatibility Evaluation and Hierarchical Framework Design
body: Speculative decoding and quantization effectively accelerate memory-bound inference of large language models. Speculative decoding mitigates the memory bandwidth bottleneck by verifying multiple tokens within a single forward pass, which increases computational effort. Quantization achieves this optimization by compressing weights and activations into lower bit-widths and also reduces computations via low-bit matrix multiplications. To further leverage their strengths, we investigate the integration of these two techniques. Surprisingly, experiments applying the advanced speculative decoding method EAGLE-2 to various quantized models reveal that the memory benefits from 4-bit weight quantization are diminished by the computational load from speculative decoding. Specifically, verifying a tree-style draft incurs significantly more time overhead than a single-token forward pass on 4-bit weight quantized models. This finding led to our new speculative decoding design: a hierarchical framework that employs a small model as an intermediate stage to turn tree-style drafts into sequence drafts, leveraging the memory access benefits of the target quantized model. Experimental results show that our hierarchical approach achieves a 2.78times speedup across various tasks for the 4-bit weight Llama-3-70B model on an A100 GPU, outperforming EAGLE-2 by 1.31times. Code available at https://github.com/AI9Stars/SpecMQuant.

title: Speculative Speculative Decoding
body: Autoregressive decoding is bottlenecked by its sequential nature. Speculative decoding has become a standard way to accelerate inference by using a fast draft model to predict upcoming tokens from a slower target model, and then verifying them in parallel with a single target model forward pass. However, speculative decoding itself relies on a sequential dependence between speculation and verification. We introduce speculative speculative decoding (SSD) to parallelize these operations. While a verification is ongoing, the draft model predicts likely verification outcomes and prepares speculations pre-emptively for them. If the actual verification outcome is then in the predicted set, a speculation can be returned immediately, eliminating drafting overhead entirely. We identify three key challenges presented by speculative speculative decoding, and suggest principled methods to solve each. The result is Saguaro, an optimized SSD algorithm. Our implementation is up to 2x faster than optimized speculative decoding baselines and up to 5x faster than autoregressive decoding with open source inference engines.

title: FASER: Fine-Grained Phase Management for Speculative Decoding in Dynamic LLM Serving
body:
Speculative decoding (SD) is a widely used approach for accelerating decode-heavy LLM inference workloads. While online inference workloads are highly dynamic, existing SD systems are rigid and take a coarse-grained approach to SD management. They typically set the speculative token length for an entire batch and serialize the execution of the draft and verification phases. Consequently, these systems fall short at adapting to volatile online inference traffic. Under low load, they exhibit prolonged latency because the draft phase blocks the verification phase for the entire batch, leaving GPU computing resources underutilized. Conversely, under high load, they waste computation on rejected tokens during the verification phase, overloading GPU resources.
  We introduce FASER, a novel system that features fine-grained SD phase management. First, FASER minimizes computational waste by dynamically adjusting the speculative length for each request within a continuous batch and by performing early pruning of rejected tokens inside the verification phase. Second, FASER breaks the verification phase into frontiers, or chunks, to overlap them with the draft phase. This overlap is achieved via fine-grained spatial multiplexing with minimal resource interference. Our FASER prototype in vLLM improves throughput by up to 53% and reduces latency by up to 1.92times compared to state-of-the-art systems.

title: Overcoming Joint Intractability with Lossless Hierarchical Speculative Decoding
body: Verification is a key bottleneck in improving inference speed while maintaining distribution fidelity in Speculative Decoding. Recent work has shown that sequence-level verification leads to a higher number of accepted tokens compared to token-wise verification. However, existing solutions often rely on surrogate approximations or are constrained by partial information, struggling with joint intractability. In this work, we propose Hierarchical Speculative Decoding (HSD), a provably lossless verification method that significantly boosts the expected number of accepted tokens and overcomes joint intractability by balancing excess and deficient probability mass across accessible branches. Our extensive large-scale experiments demonstrate that HSD yields consistent improvements in acceptance rates across diverse model families and benchmarks. Moreover, its strong explainability and generality make it readily integrable into a wide range of speculative decoding frameworks. Notably, integrating HSD into EAGLE-3 yields over a 12% performance gain, establishing state-of-the-art decoding efficiency without compromising distribution fidelity. Code is available at https://github.com/ZhouYuxuanYX/Hierarchical-Speculative-Decoding.

title: ExpertFlow: Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Inference via Predictive Expert Caching and Token Scheduling
body: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models can outperform dense large language models at similar computation by activating only a small set of experts per token. However, stacking many expert modules introduces substantial parameter memory, which makes MoE models difficult to deploy in memory-constrained environments such as single-GPU devices. Offloading alleviates this issue by storing inactive experts in CPU memory and loading them on demand, but existing methods remain limited: static caches disregard input-dependent routing, and methods that train separate models to predict expert usage ahead of time are often inaccurate or require significant training cost. We propose ExpertFlow, a lightweight MoE inference system that addresses this routing dependency through three coordinated components: 1) a transformer-based routing path predictor that estimates expert usage across all MoE layers in a single forward pass, 2) a token scheduler that groups tokens with similar predicted routes to improve expert utilization, and 3) a predictive expert cache that loads only the required experts while correcting mispredictions at runtime. Together, these components enable efficient expert loading and execution, reducing GPU memory usage by up to 93.72% and improving inference throughput by up to 10x over strong offloading baselines on a single GPU.

title: Not All Experts are Equal: Efficient Expert Pruning and Skipping for Mixture-of-Experts Large Language Models
body: A pivotal advancement in the progress of large language models (LLMs) is the emergence of the Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLMs. Compared to traditional LLMs, MoE LLMs can achieve higher performance with fewer parameters, but it is still hard to deploy them due to their immense parameter sizes. Different from previous weight pruning methods that rely on specifically designed hardware, this paper mainly aims to enhance the deployment efficiency of MoE LLMs by introducing plug-and-play expert-level sparsification techniques. Specifically, we propose, for the first time to our best knowledge, post-training approaches for task-agnostic and task-specific expert pruning and skipping of MoE LLMs, tailored to improve deployment efficiency while maintaining model performance across a wide range of tasks. Extensive experiments show that our proposed methods can simultaneously reduce model sizes and increase the inference speed, while maintaining satisfactory performance. Data and code will be available at https://github.com/Lucky-Lance/Expert_Sparsity.

title: GraphMETRO: Mitigating Complex Graph Distribution Shifts via Mixture of Aligned Experts
body: Graph data are inherently complex and heterogeneous, leading to a high natural diversity of distributional shifts. However, it remains unclear how to build machine learning architectures that generalize to the complex distributional shifts naturally occurring in the real world. Here, we develop GraphMETRO, a Graph Neural Network architecture that models natural diversity and captures complex distributional shifts. GraphMETRO employs a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture with a gating model and multiple expert models, where each expert model targets a specific distributional shift to produce a referential representation w.r.t. a reference model, and the gating model identifies shift components. Additionally, we design a novel objective that aligns the representations from different expert models to ensure reliable optimization. GraphMETRO achieves state-of-the-art results on four datasets from the GOOD benchmark, which is comprised of complex and natural real-world distribution shifts, improving by 67% and 4.2% on the WebKB and Twitch datasets. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Wuyxin/GraphMETRO.

title: Mixtures of Experts Models
body: Mixtures of experts models provide a framework in which covariates may be included in mixture models. This is achieved by modelling the parameters of the mixture model as functions of the concomitant covariates. Given their mixture model foundation, mixtures of experts models possess a diverse range of analytic uses, from clustering observations to capturing parameter heterogeneity in cross-sectional data. This chapter focuses on delineating the mixture of experts modelling framework and demonstrates the utility and flexibility of mixtures of experts models as an analytic tool.

title:
Capacity-Aware Inference: Mitigating the Straggler Effect in Mixture of
  Experts
body:
The Mixture of Experts (MoE) is an effective architecture for scaling large
language models by leveraging sparse expert activation, optimizing the
trade-off between performance and efficiency. However, under expert
parallelism, MoE suffers from inference inefficiencies due to imbalanced
token-to-expert assignment, where some experts are overloaded while others
remain underutilized. This imbalance leads to poor resource utilization and
increased latency, as the most burdened expert dictates the overall delay, a
phenomenon we define as the \textit{Straggler Effect}. To mitigate
this, we propose Capacity-Aware Inference, including two key techniques: (1)
\textit{Capacity-Aware Token Drop}, which discards overloaded tokens
to regulate the maximum latency of MoE, and (2) \textit{Capacity-Aware
Token Reroute}, which reallocates overflowed tokens to underutilized experts,
balancing the token distribution. These techniques collectively optimize both
high-load and low-load expert utilization, leading to a more efficient MoE
inference pipeline. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our
methods, showing significant improvements in inference efficiency, e.g., 0.2\%
average performance increase and a 1.94times inference speedup on
Mixtral-8times7B-Instruct.

title: GW-MoE: Resolving Uncertainty in MoE Router with Global Workspace Theory
body:
Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) has been demonstrated as an efficient method to
scale up models. By dynamically and sparsely selecting activated experts, MoE
can effectively reduce computational costs. Despite the success, we observe
that many tokens in the MoE models have uncertain routing results. These tokens
have nearly equal scores for choosing each expert, and we demonstrate that this
uncertainty can lead to incorrect selections. Inspired by the Global Workspace
Theory (GWT), we propose a new fine-tuning method, GW-MoE, to address this
issue. The core idea is to broadcast the uncertain tokens across experts during
fine-tuning. Therefore, these tokens can acquire the necessary knowledge from
any expert during inference and become less sensitive to the choice. GW-MoE
does not introduce additional inference overhead. We validate that GW can
mitigate the uncertain problem and consistently improve in different tasks
(text classification, question answering, summarization, code generation, and
mathematical problem solving) and model sizes (650M and 8B parameters).

title: Mixture-of-Experts with Expert Choice Routing
body:
Sparsely-activated Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models allow the number of
parameters to greatly increase while keeping the amount of computation for a
given token or a given sample unchanged. However, a poor expert routing
strategy (e.g. one resulting in load imbalance) can cause certain experts to be
under-trained, leading to an expert being under or over-specialized. Prior work
allocates a fixed number of experts to each token using a top-k function
regardless of the relative importance of different tokens. To address this, we
propose a heterogeneous mixture-of-experts employing an expert choice method.
Instead of letting tokens select the top-k experts, we have experts selecting
the top-k tokens. As a result, each token can be routed to a variable number of
experts and each expert can have a fixed bucket size. We systematically study
pre-training speedups using the same computational resources of the Switch
Transformer top-1 and GShard top-2 gating of prior work and find that our
method improves training convergence time by more than 2x. For the same
computational cost, our method demonstrates higher performance in fine-tuning
11 selected tasks in the GLUE and SuperGLUE benchmarks. For a smaller
activation cost, our method outperforms the T5 dense model in 7 out of the 11
tasks.
